articles.title: Tanzania and World Bank Map Central Corridor Investment Opportunities in Agriculture, Logistics, Mining, and Tourism - TanzaniaInvest
articles.summary: Tanzania and World Bank Map Central Corridor Investment Opportunities in Agriculture, Logistics, Mining, and Tourism  TanzaniaInvest
articles.full_text:
Tanzania and the World Bank are identifying Central Corridor investment opportunities in agriculture, mining, tourism, and logistics, while UNDP prepares projects for a June 2027 investment conference.
The Minister for Finance, Ambassador Khamis Mussa Omar, met the Managing Director of Operations at the World Bank, Anna Bjerde, in Bangkok, Thailand, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Annual Meetings held from 12 to 18 October 2026.
The talks focused on accelerating economic development through infrastructure construction, job creation, and private sector investment, with Omar stressing that progress should be measured by higher production, wider employment opportunities, and rising incomes rather than growth indicators alone.
The meeting also discussed the Central Corridor as a key transport route able to strengthen regional trade, ease the movement of goods, and connect Tanzania’s markets with neighbouring countries.
Omar described tourism as a sector able to create jobs quickly, noting that opportunities around the great lakes and along the coast remain underused and should be developed to raise tourist arrivals and open more employment.
Bjerde said job creation is the World Bank’s top priority in supporting economic development, and that the Bank is advancing a strategy to strengthen micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), which account for a large share of business activity and employment.
To support this, the two sides discussed shifting small business lending from reliance on asset collateral towards assessment of business cash flow, so that firms obtain capital according to their capacity to generate revenue, grow, and add jobs.
Bjerde also commended Tanzania’s focus on building an industrial economy through agriculture, livestock, and mineral value addition, a strategy that aims to keep more of the value of national resources inside the country and reach a 40% value addition target.
On education, the World Bank urged a focus on quality and learning outcomes rather than enrolment numbers alone, including better teaching methods and education systems that use artificial intelligence to prepare young people for the global economy and labour market.
World Bank officials said they intend to speed up project preparation and implementation by cutting the time needed before projects start, and the Bank is drafting a special plan to identify and remove the bottlenecks that delay delivery.
Both sides agreed to continue their strategic partnership to accelerate Tanzania’s development priorities, and the Bank encouraged the Government to keep presenting its development needs with confidence so that cooperation and support can be used effectively.
The World Bank Vice President for Eastern and Southern Africa, Dr. Ndiamé Diop, the Minister for Finance of Zanzibar, Dr. Juma Malik Akil, the Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Finance, Dr. Natu El-Maamry Mwamba, and the Permanent Secretary in the President’s Office for Planning, Dr. Tausi Kida, also attended the meeting.
In a separate meeting in Bangkok, Omar held talks with the Administrator of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), Alexander De Croo, a former Prime Minister of Belgium, on youth employment, education, investment attraction, and private sector growth.
Omar said youth employment is a key development priority because young people make up a large share of the population, which calls for strategies that equip them with skills, capital, technology, and markets to become self-employed or employable.
“Employment and youth issues are very broad. We need to ensure that young people gain the right skills, affordable start-up capital, technology, knowledge, and access to markets so that they can participate fully in production and national development,” Omar stated.
Omar added that the Government will keep investing in education and education infrastructure to meet demand from population growth, which continues to raise requirements for schools, teachers, books, and other facilities.
He explained that Tanzania continues working with development partners to identify investment opportunities and prepare projects able to attract domestic and foreign investors.
The Government and the World Bank are currently mapping trade and investment opportunities along the Central Corridor, which links the Port of Dar es Salaam with the interior through transport infrastructure including the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR), with potential to extend the opportunities to Rwanda.
“This corridor has great opportunities in the agriculture, mining, tourism, and transport sectors and in the development of transport and supply centres (logistics centres), which can attract investment and stimulate production as well as employment,” Omar noted.
Omar also said the Government is improving the business and investment environment, including through recommendations from committees formed to examine challenges in the tax system and in the conduct of business.
De Croo expressed UNDP’s readiness to keep supporting Tanzania’s development agenda, including empowering young people, strengthening skills, and expanding economic opportunities in partnership with the Government, the private sector, and other development institutions.
He said investment should be viewed as a long-term development strategy, particularly in the use of natural resources, including rare minerals needed for the global energy transition.
De Croo commended the Government for preparing the Integrated National Financing Framework (INFF), which he said will help improve the availability and coordination of resources for financing development priorities.
He explained that UNDP, together with the Tanzania Investment Growth Facility (TIGF), aims to turn the identified opportunities into projects backed by documented plans and robust financial and commercial structures able to attract investors ahead of the investment conference expected in Tanzania in June 2027.
“We are ready to work with Tanzania in preparing for that conference and in seeking financing for sustainable infrastructure and blue economy projects through partnership with the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), with the aim of accelerating project implementation and increasing the contribution of investment to economic growth and the prosperity of citizens,” De Croo stated.
The meeting was also attended by Akil, Mwamba, the Permanent Secretary in the Zanzibar Ministry of Finance, Aboud Hassan Mwinyi, and Enock Koola, a Member of Parliament and member of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Budget, alongside other Government and UNDP officials.
The Central Corridor is Tanzania’s main transport and trade route, connecting the Port of Dar es Salaam with the interior and with landlocked markets including Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda, Zambia, Malawi, and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
In August 2026, the Government and the World Bank finalized technical preparations for KAZI MPA, the Catalyzing Jobs and Resilient Growth in the Central Corridor Multiphase Programmatic Approach, which targets youth employment and private sector-led growth along the route.
During a visit to Tanzania that included talks on 20 August 2026, Diop said the Bank’s next phase of cooperation would aim to transform the corridor from a transit route into a fully fledged economic corridor.
TIGF is a platform hosted by the Economic and Social Research Foundation (ESRF) and supported by UNDP to strengthen project preparation, mobilise capital, and fast-track investment in priority sectors, and it was launched during the Tanzania Investment Summit 2026 held in Arusha on 1 and 2 June 2026.
At that summit, the Government presented 60 investment-ready public projects worth USD 6.35 billion, up from USD 2.85 billion at an earlier stage.

articles.title: AfCFTA: Ghana exported to 47 African countries in 2025 - CitiNewsroom.com
articles.summary: AfCFTA: Ghana exported to 47 African countries in 2025  CitiNewsroom.com
articles.full_text:
The National Coordinator of the National AfCFTA Coordination Office, Dode Seidu, has underscored the benefits of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), citing Ghana’s export of non-traditional goods to 47 African countries in 2025 as evidence of the country’s progress under the trade agreement.
Speaking on the Citi Breakfast Show on Wednesday, October 21, Mr Seidu said Ghana had made significant strides in implementing the agreement through initiatives across the public and private sectors, although more work was needed to maximise its benefits.
He explained that Ghana was the first country to establish a national coordination office to support the implementation of the agreement, which requires several government agencies and institutions to integrate AfCFTA into their operations.
According to him, various institutions have since taken steps to align their activities with the agreement, demonstrating the country’s readiness to expand trade and investment across the continent.
Mr Seidu cited the Ghana Investment Promotion Centre’s establishment of an AfCFTA focal desk to facilitate and attract intra-African investment as one of the measures supporting the initiative.
“If you go to Ghana’s Promotion Authority, which are all agents under the Ministry of Trade, you’ve seen clear signals. For example, if you look at the annual export NTE non traditional export report issued by Ghana’s for promotion authority in 2025, we exported to 47 African countries under the AFCFTA.”
Despite these developments, Mr Seidu cautioned that significant work remained, particularly in expanding awareness of the agreement among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
He noted that many SMEs were yet to understand the opportunities available under AfCFTA, making it necessary to intensify efforts to educate businesses and encourage their participation in the continental market.

articles.title: Artisanal and small-scale mining sector generated $10.8bn in foreign exchange in 2025 — GoldBod - Modern Ghana
articles.summary: Artisanal and small-scale mining sector generated $10.8bn in foreign exchange in 2025 — GoldBod  Modern Ghana
articles.full_text:
The Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod), Sammy Gyamfi, says the artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) sector generated $10.8 billion in foreign exchange (FX) for Ghana in 2025, following reforms aimed at bringing gold previously lost to smuggling and illegal trade into the formal economy.
He said gold exports from the ASM sector also increased significantly in volume, rising from 63 tonnes in 2024 to nearly 104 tonnes in 2025.
“More importantly, the ASM gold sector in 2025 generated $10.8 billion in foreign exchange for the country,” Mr Gyamfi said in a keynote address at the 2026 African Minerals Policy Forum in Accra last Monday.
The forum, dubbed “Mining in Motion”, was held on the theme: “From Gold Production to National Prosperity: Ghana's GoldBod Model for Mineral Sovereignty and Value Addition.”
Mr Gyamfi said the foreign exchange generated from ASM gold supported reserve accumulation and currency stability, contributing to the cedi's 41 per cent appreciation against the US dollar in 2025.
The conference was organised by the Ashanti Green Initiative, with the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources serving as the principal convening partner and support from the World Bank, the World Gold Council and the African Union.
The event brought together Liberia's Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung, former UK Deputy Prime Minister Dominic Raab, Lands and Natural Resources Minister Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, Environment Minister Dr Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann, African Union officials and ministers from Guinea, Tanzania, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Malawi and Liberia.
GoldBod outlines reforms
Mr Gyamfi said GoldBod had introduced a four-tier licensing system, transparent pricing, digital stock-booking, official receipts and increased state-funded liquidity for local gold purchases as part of efforts to formalise gold trading and curb smuggling and under-declaration.
The Board had also deployed a task force and inspectorate across the country to monitor compliance and gather intelligence on illegal gold trading and smuggling.
According to him, the measures were designed to address long-standing leakages in the ASM sector, where significant quantities of gold had been lost to the formal economy through smuggling, under-declaration and informal cross-border trade.
Push for local refining
Mr Gyamfi said GoldBod was also focused on retaining more value from Ghana's gold by expanding local refining.
He said 18.7 tonnes of gold had been refined locally since August 1, 2026, with 5.4 tonnes out of the 5.7 tonnes of ASM gold purchased in October refined locally.
He said GoldBod had entered into refining agreements with two privately owned refineries, Gold Coast Refinery and Royal Ghana Gold Refinery.
“These two refineries have progressively and cumulatively refined 25 tonnes of ASM gold purchased and exported by the GoldBod this year. This represents about 30 per cent of total ASM gold exports (85.4 tonnes) from year to date,” he stated.
Mr Gyamfi said GoldBod was pursuing a policy shift from the export of raw minerals towards achieving zero raw mineral exports by 2030.
GoldBod targets more jobs and support for miners
The GoldBod CEO said the Board's institutional, licensing and value-addition reforms had created 4,866 direct jobs, comprising 361 public-sector and 4,505 private-sector positions.
He said additional employment opportunities were expected to emerge across the gold value chain as the reforms progressed.
Mr Gyamfi announced that GoldBod would introduce an ASM Formalisation and Financing Support Programme next year in partnership with the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources and the University of Mines and Technology (UMAT).
The programme will receive technical support from Rand Refinery of South Africa and is expected to increase production, revenue and employment while reducing operating costs and environmental degradation.
He also disclosed that GoldBod was procuring a blockchain-based traceability system to track gold from legitimate sources throughout the supply chain and strengthen responsible sourcing.
Mr Gyamfi called for greater cooperation among African countries on mineral governance, arguing that national-level reforms alone could not effectively tackle cross-border smuggling and other challenges affecting mineral markets.
He said Ghana's experience could help inform a broader continental approach aimed at enabling African countries to retain more value from their natural resources.

articles.title: Obasanjo Says Tinubu, ECOWAS Mishandling Of Niger Coup Pushed Three Sahel Nations Out Of Bloc - Sahara Reporters
articles.summary: Obasanjo Says Tinubu, ECOWAS Mishandling Of Niger Coup Pushed Three Sahel Nations Out Of Bloc  Sahara Reporters
articles.full_text:
Obasanjo made the remarks during an interview at the Harvard Kennedy School’s Institute of Politics, monitored by SaharaReporters on Tuesday night, while assessing insecurity and political instability across Africa.
Former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo has criticised the handling of the military coup in Niger Republic by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), saying the regional bloc’s response contributed to a deterioration in relations and the withdrawal of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso from the organisation.
Obasanjo made the remarks during an interview at the Harvard Kennedy School’s Institute of Politics, monitored by SaharaReporters on Tuesday night, while assessing insecurity and political instability across Africa.
He said West Africa had experienced renewed instability following coups in the three countries, with conflicts continuing to affect the region.
“We seem to be doing fairly well until we started having a spate of coups again. Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger Republic,” Obasanjo said.
The former president specifically criticised the handling of the coup in Niger, saying the response contributed to the wider divisions within the regional bloc.
“We were still managing to keep our regional organisation intact, ECOWAS, until the coup in Niger Republic, when I believe the way ECOWAS as an organisation handled it, and Nigeria as the leader in ECOWAS reacted, made three of the members of ECOWAS, Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger Republic, rebel,” he said.
“I think it was a bit of a sort of rebellion and they got out of ECOWAS and declared themselves Alliance of the Sahel.”
He argued that the situation had changed significantly for ECOWAS since the coups, noting that the regional bloc was still pursuing efforts to bring the three countries back into its fold.
“Since then, things have not been the same for ECOWAS as a region, and things have not been the same. There has been conflict in Mali, conflict in Burkina Faso, conflict in Niger Republic. An effort to bring them back into ECOWAS is still being pursued,” he said.
In July 2023, Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu became chairman of the ECOWAS Authority of Heads of State and Government and vowed a firm response to military coups in West Africa.
Following the July 26, 2023 coup in Niger, which ousted President Mohamed Bazoum, Tinubu led ECOWAS in condemning the takeover, imposing sanctions and demanding the restoration of constitutional rule. The regional bloc also threatened possible military intervention and activated its standby force, but ultimately pursued diplomacy rather than launching an operation.
The proposed intervention deepened divisions within the region. Mali and Burkina Faso, both under military rule, warned that an attack on Niger would be considered an attack on them and pledged to support the Nigerien junta.
In September 2023, the three countries formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), a mutual-defence pact intended to strengthen their security cooperation and reduce their dependence on ECOWAS and Western-backed arrangements.
In January 2024, Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger announced their withdrawal from ECOWAS, accusing the organisation of unfair treatment, foreign influence and failing to address insecurity in the Sahel.
Obasanjo’s comments came as he described Africa as experiencing one of its worst periods of armed conflict, violence and insecurity since independence.
“I think I would be right to say that since independence, because we know the period of the war of independence and things, but since independence, maybe things have not been as bad as this in terms of wars and conflicts and violence in Africa,” he said.
Obasanjo said insecurity was not confined to West Africa, pointing to the conflicts in Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Ethiopia.
He described Sudan’s crisis as one of the continent’s greatest humanitarian disasters, citing the involvement of external powers in the conflict.
“And then now we have the one that is worse in Sudan, where you have two parties in Sudan, one supported by Egypt, essentially, another one supported by UAE, and one of the greatest humanitarian disasters in Africa as of today,” he said.
On the DRC, Obasanjo said the country had not experienced lasting peace since 1960 and warned that the situation was deteriorating.
“Democratic Republic of Congo, since 1960, has not known real peace. And the worst is already developing in Democratic Republic of Congo now, with one government in Kinshasa and another government building up in Goma, eastern Congo,” he said.
He added that the conflict between the DRC and Rwanda had persisted for more than 30 years.
“The situation, of course, between Rwanda and DRC, has been on for more than 30 years.”
Summarising the security situation across Africa, Obasanjo said no region was free from some form of conflict, violence or insecurity.
“There’s no region in Africa that hasn’t got an element of war, but conflict. Africa is ridden with conflict. There’s no region which hasn’t got an element of war,” he said.
“No region with violence in one form or the other. No region without insecurity of one kind or the other. So that’s the picture that I can paint for Africa.”
Obasanjo also argued that African countries should be able to seek help from international partners when needed, saying the principle of “African solutions to African problems” should not rule out external assistance.
He called for the principle of subsidiarity to guide decisions about how conflicts are addressed, with the level of intervention determined by the nature of each crisis.
“And we always talk of two things. One is African solution for African problem. Another one is subsidiarity. And I believe the two must go together,” he said.

articles.title: Exclusive / Washington won’t say what it wants on AGOA, says South Africa ambassador - Semafor
articles.summary: Exclusive / Washington won’t say what it wants on AGOA, says South Africa ambassador  Semafor
articles.full_text:
South Africa’s ambassador to the US says Washington has repeatedly rejected Pretoria’s trade offers without explaining what it wants instead. His complaint comes a day after President Cyril Ramaphosa told South Africans to brace for losing duty-free access under the African Growth and Opportunity Act.
“It’s not helpful when we hear the answer is, ‘that’s not good enough,’” Roelf Meyer told Semafor. “It would have been more helpful if we could hear, ‘what is not good enough?’”
The US Congress extended AGOA to 2028 last month, but the White House reviews country eligibility every year. Removing South Africa from Jan. 1 would require notice to Congress and Pretoria 60 days ahead, so a decision is expected by early November. That scenario has become a distinct possibility after nearly two years of a worsening relationship between Washington and Africa’s largest economy.
Meyer, who took up the post this year after more than a year without a South African ambassador in Washington, describes relations with the Trump administration as a “stalemate.” “I’m not satisfied about where we find ourselves,” he said.
The deeper rift, he suggested, is ideological. Meyer said he read the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 early and saw a “deviation” from the Republican Party he knew in the 1980s. Asked why Pretoria’s rebuttals of white genocide claims aren’t landing, he said either Washington hasn’t heard him clearly, or there is “a fundamental ideological difference.”
Meyer helped lead the apartheid government’s side opposite Ramaphosa in the talks that ended white minority rule. He says those negotiations worked because both sides were prepared to talk. “That is my experience, the difference here,” he said. “It’s hard to find a basis for real dialogue.”
Yet he also signaled flexibility on the policy irritant most cited in Washington. Black EconomicEmpowerment rules in mining and telecoms “still leave room for further adjustments,” he said, adding that discussions are underway with companies looking to invest.
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Yinka: President Cyril Ramaphosa warned South Africans to prepare for the possibility that the country could lose its AGOA trade benefits. How confident are you that South Africa will remain eligible?
Roelf Meyer: It is difficult to say because we have not had a clear response on AGOA and the eligibility question. There is a lot of speculation about the final result, and I don’t think it serves any purpose to add to that.
From the South African side, we believe we have given clear enough answers. We would like an opportunity to hear where the shortcomings are in the US assessment. It is not helpful when the answer is simply, “That’s not good enough.” We need to know what is not good enough so we can address it from a negotiating perspective.
I think the president is being realistic, so nobody is completely surprised if things go in the wrong direction. But he is also mindful that it would be better if we could stay in.
What are the main sticking points in the negotiations?
There are difficult issues on which South Africa cannot simply agree with everything the US is asking. We have local interests to consider, particularly in the poultry and pork industries.
These are longstanding, technical issues involving imports and exports. Local producers react when imports affect their production or export potential, and experts from our respective departments have been negotiating with them for an extended period.
But there are also political issues. The US government has raised a number of concerns about South Africa over the past 18 months, and those weigh on the discussions too.
How much of your time is spent on those political disputes, as opposed to trade and investment?
I think it is 50-50. The political relationship has been tense since the executive order on South Africa in February last year, which covered a number of issues and led to the five asks or demands.
My responsibility is both political and commercial. It is about how we keep trade going and expand it.
Do you think the tensions will ease, or have the problems become more entrenched?
It is difficult to say. Some of the geopolitical issues concerning the US were already present under the previous administration, and some concerns coming from Capitol Hill are bipartisan.
Part of the embassy’s job is to address misunderstandings and relay US concerns to our government. We may make assumptions in Pretoria that are wrong, too. It is my responsibility to give the president and government as clear a picture as possible.
Could changes to Black Economic Empowerment policies help attract more investment, particularly in mining and telecommunications?
The BEE framework has evolved from an initial focus on equity toward equity-equivalence measures. Many companies have adjusted to those measures and invested on that basis.
There is still room for further adjustments, particularly in mining and telecommunications. Those sectors have a different character under the current framework, and we discuss possible changes internally and with companies that want to invest.
You have been in Washington for about five months. How would you sum up the state of the relationship?
South Africa had no representation in Washington for some period before I arrived, so there is a lot of catching up to do across the executive and legislative branches. I think we have started to make progress.
But we are still in a stalemate with the executive. I am not satisfied with where we find ourselves. As long as this situation persists, further attention is required, and policy positions may need to change.
My task is to establish exactly what the issues are and report back to Pretoria, while convincing decision-makers here that Pretoria’s intent is to establish a solid relationship.
Does that mean engaging with conservative organizations such as the Heritage Foundation to understand the thinking behind the administration’s policies?
It is important to understand the roots of this thinking and the American context. Some decisions are coming from a framework different from the one I knew in the past.
I know the framework of the 1980s very well. It was relatively simple to understand: Republican and Democrat. Today, it is more splintered, with fundamental ideological issues at stake. My responsibility is to understand those issues and relay that understanding to Pretoria. I have to speak to a wide range of people, including those outside the administration, to understand what lies behind policy positions directed against South Africa.
You have rejected claims that white South Africans are victims of genocide, yet the US has moved ahead with a refugee policy centered on that narrative. Why do you think your arguments are not getting through?
There could be two explanations. One is that they have not heard me clearly. The other is that there is a fundamental ideological difference.
I became aware of Project 2025 long before I knew I would take this role. I looked at it and said to myself that this was not the material I knew from the Republican Party. I could see a deviation.
But I would not make a broader accusation, because I do not have proof of that. My presence here is not to represent a particular faction. I am here to represent South Africa.
You helped negotiate the end of apartheid. Is dealing with Washington now harder than those negotiations?
The starting point in those negotiations was that we were prepared to talk. That led gradually to serious talks, dialogue and negotiations. We were prepared to listen to each other.
That is the difference in my experience here. It is hard to find a basis for real dialogue. I am not saying one side is right and the other is wrong. But if we want to build a way forward between South Africa and the US, we need to develop that dialogue. I would like to see South Africa and the United States become good partners. For that to happen, we need proper dialogue.

articles.title: Ghana to end unprocessed mineral exports by 2030 - African Business
articles.summary: Ghana to end unprocessed mineral exports by 2030  African Business
articles.full_text:
Ghana, Africa’s largest gold exporter and a major producer of minerals such as manganese, bauxite (pictured) and diamonds, has announced plans to end exports of unprocessed minerals by 2030, as African countries increasingly seek ways to capture more economic value from their natural resources.
Speaking at a mining conference in Accra on 19 October, Ghana’s president John Mahama said, “I’ve set a clear goal that by 2030, raw minerals should no longer leave our shores.”
“Our bauxite, manganese, iron, lithium and other minerals must support processing and industrial development here at home,” he added.
Africa has emerged as one of the world’s most strategically important markets for critical minerals, and is believed to be home to 30% of critical mineral reserves globally. Minerals such as manganese, of which Africa accounts for more than 75% of global production, are vital for the production of technologies such as electric vehicle batteries and are therefore seen as essential for the green transition.
Ghana joins other African nations
Despite this, many African countries have struggled to capture the full economic value associated with critical minerals, which are mostly exported raw for processing and manufacturing overseas. Ghana would join a growing cohort of African countries, among them Zimbabwe, DRC and Namibia, which have also announced export restrictions on raw minerals.
Earlier this year, Hanan Morsy, deputy executive secretary and chief economist of the UN Economic Commission for Africa, stated that the continent captures less than 5% of the associated value added from critical minerals. The African Development Bank (AfDB) has suggested that, by processing minerals domestically, the continent could generate an additional $24bn in annual GDP, boost annual exports by $32bn and create 2.3m new jobs.
However, some analysts are sceptical that export bans will help achieve this goal. Tresor Chovu, founder and CEO at Temple Fortune Capital, a mining-focused investment and advisory firm, tells African Business that “good intentions do not necessarily lead to good results.”
“In order to be able to process minerals successfully, you need a stable power supply, you need the technology, you need the workforce and people who are able to operate the technology,” he says. “And then you need local ownership and people that either have the capital or the partnerships with international companies to set up processing plants. After that you need to organise the supply chain.”
“I suspect they are giving themselves four years to get these prerequisites in place, but it is a very difficult target to meet.”
Chovu also suggests the ban could prove to be counterproductive by potentially deterring foreign investors from setting up operations in Ghana.
“It could have an impact on foreign direct investment and investor sentiment, especially for newcomers who want to enter Ghana and will now have to consider the cost of processing as well as mining,” he says. “Existing international mining companies will also have to get something back in return if they are going to set up processing plans in Ghana: they will want tax breaks and the like.”
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), an organisation of 38 mostly wealthy countries, has also warned about the potential consequences of such measures. “Export bans and quotes are technically not permitted under WTO [World Trade Organization] rules unless an exemption is met,” the organisation noted in an 18 October policy paper, while noting that “export restrictions impact the domestic mining sector of producing countries in several ways.”
“First, they lower export volumes, which impacts export earnings and government revenues from the sector. Second, they can push down domestic mineral prices to below international prices (due to lower demand domestically), which benefits local processors who can buy minerals inputs more cheaply, but harms mining companies… third, such restrictions can also prompt technological innovations away from minerals subject to export restrictions or other supply chain risk.”

articles.title: Pakistan’s Copper Exports to China: A Growing Part of the CPEC 2.0 Story - The Daily CPEC
articles.summary: Pakistan’s Copper Exports to China: A Growing Part of the CPEC 2.0 Story  The Daily CPEC
articles.full_text:
Pakistan copper exports to China recorded strong growth in 2026, highlighting new opportunities under CPEC 2.0. Refined unwrought copper exports increased by 68.51% between January and August, while exports of unrefined copper and copper anodes for electrolytic refining rose by 44.14%.
Overall, Pakistan’s exports to China increased by 40.51%. They reached $2.386 billion, compared with $1.698 billion during the same period in 2025, according to the Associated Press of Pakistan.
These figures highlight a growing trend in Pakistan-China trade. Copper is becoming an increasingly important part of Pakistan’s export relationship with China. As a result, it could play a larger role in the next phase of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, known as CPEC 2.0.
However, export growth raises an important question. Can Pakistan capture more value from its copper before it reaches Chinese manufacturers?
China Is a Major Market for Pakistani Copper
Pakistan copper exports to China have become an important part of the country’s bilateral trade relationship.
World Bank trade data show that Pakistan exported $791.5 million worth of refined unwrought copper products worldwide in 2024. China accounted for $786.6 million of that total.
Pakistan shipped more than 76.6 million kilograms of these products to China, according to the World Integrated Trade Solution (WITS).
This concentration highlights China’s importance to Pakistan’s copper industry. The latest export figures also suggest that an established trade relationship is gaining momentum.
Minerals have become an important part of this relationship. The Daily CPEC reported that Pakistan’s mineral exports to China reached $1.14 billion in 2025. Copper accounted for a major share of these exports.
The latest figures suggest that this momentum continued into 2026.
Muhammad Imran, Pakistan’s Trade and Investment Counsellor at the Consulate General in Guangzhou, linked the wider export growth to Chinese industrial demand for refined metals. He also highlighted gains in agriculture and textiles, according to the Associated Press of Pakistan.
Therefore, copper should be viewed as part of a broader shift in Pakistan’s export sector. It is not merely an isolated mining success.
Why China’s Copper Demand Matters
Growing demand for industrial metals creates new opportunities for Pakistan copper exports to China.
China plays a major role in the global copper industry. The metal is essential for electrical equipment, power transmission, construction, and electronics. It also supports technologies linked to electrification.
China has a large copper-processing industry and a substantial manufacturing base. This creates opportunities for suppliers that can provide reliable copper shipments.
Recent market developments also highlight the importance of secure supplies. Reuters reported in October 2026 that Chinese regulators sought copper supply commitments linked to Anglo American’s proposed merger with Teck Resources. The development reflected concerns about copper feedstock availability among Chinese smelters.
China’s refined copper trade is also changing. Reuters reported earlier in 2026 that China’s net imports of refined copper fell during the first half of the year. High prices and shifting global trade flows contributed to this change.
For Pakistan, these developments create both opportunities and challenges.
China offers a large market for Pakistani copper. However, exporting basic copper products limits the value Pakistan can retain from downstream manufacturing.
The key challenge is to move beyond supplying raw materials. Pakistan must also explore opportunities in processing, industrial production, and higher-value exports.
How CPEC 2.0 Could Support Copper Development
CPEC 2.0 could help Pakistan copper exports to China generate wider industrial benefits through investment in processing and manufacturing.
CPEC 2.0 could provide a framework for expanding Pakistan’s mineral industry. The focus is increasingly shifting towards industrial cooperation, technology, agriculture, and private-sector investment.
The CPEC Secretariat has identified mining as one of the sectors expected to feature prominently in the second phase.
Similarly, the Pakistan-China joint statement issued in May 2026 called for cooperation in mining and oil and gas exploration. It also highlighted industrial cooperation and technology-related sectors.
Copper fits naturally into these priorities.
Higher exports can generate foreign exchange and strengthen commercial ties with Chinese buyers. However, Pakistan could gain more by developing domestic processing and manufacturing capabilities.
For example, investment could support modern refining facilities, mineral testing, and engineering services. It could also encourage equipment manufacturing and industries that use processed copper.
These activities could create opportunities beyond extraction. They could also help Pakistani businesses participate in more stages of the copper supply chain.
The distinction is important. Exporting more copper strengthens trade. Building a domestic copper value chain could create a wider industrial impact.
Turning Mineral Resources Into Industrial Value
Pakistan has significant mineral potential, particularly in Balochistan. However, natural resources alone cannot create a competitive mining industry.
The country needs reliable geological data and modern extraction technology. It also needs processing facilities, transport links, skilled workers, and predictable investment rules.
Environmental protection and workplace safety must remain priorities throughout this process.
Pakistan and China have already established channels for mineral cooperation. The China-Pakistan Mineral Cooperation Forum, held in January 2026, provided a platform for discussing opportunities in the mining sector.
However, cooperation must lead to practical results.
Processing facilities need to be commercially viable. Transport infrastructure must connect mines with industrial centres and export markets. Local communities should also benefit from mining activity.
Furthermore, Pakistani companies need opportunities to participate in supply chains. Otherwise, much of the economic value may remain concentrated in extraction and basic processing.
These factors will determine whether rising copper exports can support long-term industrial development.
Pakistan Is Already Exporting Refined Copper
One important detail stands out in the latest trade figures. Refined unwrought copper recorded the strongest reported growth among the two copper categories discussed.
This distinction matters because refined copper has already undergone processing. It is therefore further along the production chain than copper ore.
Pakistan’s copper trade with China is not limited to the most basic stage of mineral production. The country already supplies a more commercially usable form of the metal.
WITS data also highlight Pakistan’s position in this market. In 2024, Pakistan exported more refined unwrought copper to China than several other suppliers, including South Africa, Kazakhstan, Morocco, and Indonesia, within the specific product category covered by the dataset.
This shows that China is already an established market for Pakistani refined copper.
The next challenge is to expand domestic capabilities further. Pakistan needs to assess which additional processing and manufacturing activities are commercially feasible.
Greater domestic capacity could help the country retain more value from its mineral resources. It could also create skilled jobs and support related industries.
Export Growth Does Not Guarantee Diversification
Copper is contributing to Pakistan’s wider export growth. According to the Associated Press of Pakistan, exports to China increased by nearly $688 million during the first eight months of 2026.
Refined metals, agricultural products, and textiles all contributed to the increase.
This growth is encouraging. Pakistan has long faced challenges in balancing its trade with China. Higher exports can help improve that balance and strengthen commercial relations.
However, export growth does not automatically mean greater diversification.
If a few commodities drive most of the increase, Pakistan remains exposed to price fluctuations and changes in Chinese demand. Production constraints could also affect export performance.
A stronger export strategy would build on copper while supporting other sectors.
Processed agricultural products, textiles, engineering goods, technology services, and manufactured products could broaden Pakistan’s export base.
This approach would reduce dependence on a limited range of commodities. It could also create more opportunities for domestic businesses.
What Copper Means for CPEC 2.0
Pakistan’s copper exports offer a useful way to assess the potential of CPEC 2.0.
The first phase of CPEC focused heavily on infrastructure, electricity generation, and connectivity. The second phase places greater emphasis on productive sectors, including industry, agriculture, minerals, and technology.
Copper connects several of these priorities.
It is a natural resource, an export commodity, and an essential industrial input. Its production can support mining companies, processors, engineers, transport providers, and manufacturers.
Therefore, the success of this sector should not be measured by export volumes alone.
Pakistan also needs to assess whether higher exports encourage investment in processing, technology, and industrial production. These capabilities could help domestic businesses capture more value from the country’s mineral resources.
The latest figures suggest that Chinese demand is creating opportunities for Pakistani exporters. The next step is to turn this demand into a foundation for wider economic growth.
If CPEC 2.0 aims to move Pakistan from connectivity towards productive capacity, copper could become an important test of that ambition.

articles.title: Uganda, South Africa Seek to Ease Trade and Travel Barriers, Expand Investment - ChimpReports
articles.summary: Uganda, South Africa Seek to Ease Trade and Travel Barriers, Expand Investment  ChimpReports
articles.full_text:
Uganda and South Africa have reaffirmed plans to expand trade and investment, with Kampala calling for coordinated action on non-tariff barriers, high logistics costs and regulatory hurdles affecting businesses.
The commitments emerged from the Third Session of the Joint Commission of Cooperation in Pretoria on October 20, co-chaired by South Africa’s International Relations and Cooperation Minister Ronald Lamola and Uganda’s Foreign Affairs Minister Adonia Ayebare.
“Economic cooperation remains central to relations between Uganda and South Africa,” Ayebare said.
He proposed trade missions and business forums to connect investors and enterprises, alongside efforts to address obstacles limiting commercial exchanges between the two countries.
Lamola welcomed Uganda’s emphasis on economic diplomacy, saying closer business partnerships could build on established political ties.
“Economic and Commercial Diplomacy provides an important pathway for translating strong diplomatic relations into tangible trade and investment opportunities,” he said.
The ministers considered and adopted recommendations from senior officials, identifying mining, energy, agriculture, telecommunications, tourism and manufacturing as priorities for cooperation.
Ayebare highlighted opportunities in agro-processing, manufacturing, energy infrastructure, information and communication technology, and financial services.
He also called for direct engagement between businesses to help turn these opportunities into investment.
Lamola cited the presence of South African companies in Uganda, including MTN, Standard Bank through Stanbic Bank Uganda, and Absa, as a foundation for further commercial cooperation.
The meeting followed the previous commission session in Kampala in 2022, a mid-term review in Pretoria in 2023 and President Yoweri Museveni’s state visit to South Africa that year.
The commission provides a framework for reviewing bilateral commitments and advancing cooperation.
Travel facilitation also featured in the talks, with Ayebare calling for immigration cooperation that supports legitimate travel for business, education and other economic activities.
The development comes against the backdrop of a growing public outcry over South Africa’s denial of visas to Ugandan travelers.
Ayebare welcomed South Africa’s Electronic Travel Authorisation system, citing positive results for Ugandan businesspeople and students.
In tourism, Ayebare proposed cooperation in destination marketing, hospitality training, skills development and conservation to increase visitor flows and improve the competitiveness of both destinations.
The ministers also reaffirmed their commitment to sustained political consultations, African integration and peaceful conflict resolution, including cooperation within the African Union, the United Nations and other multilateral platforms.
Both called for regular follow-up and effective implementation of agreed commitments to expand bilateral trade and investment.

articles.title: Ethiopia Joins Africa’s Cross-Border Payments Network, Opening New Opportunities For Trade And Investment - Trendsnafrica
articles.summary: Ethiopia Joins Africa’s Cross-Border Payments Network, Opening New Opportunities For Trade And Investment  Trendsnafrica
articles.full_text:
(3 Minutes Read)
Ethiopia has joined the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), a continental financial infrastructure initiative designed to make cross-border payments across Africa faster, more efficient, and cost-effective.
Operating under the auspices of the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), the African Union (AU), and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretariat, PAPSS aims to reduce transaction costs, streamline cross-border settlements, and address financial barriers to intra-African trade. Ethiopia’s membership provides a pathway for its financial institutions to connect to a broader pan-African payments network, potentially reducing reliance on traditional international payment channels that often involve additional intermediaries, longer processing times, and higher costs.
For Ethiopian exporters, importers, and investors, the system could simplify payments with African business partners and support regional commercial activity. However, the practical benefits will depend on how quickly commercial banks integrate with the platform, the currencies and payment corridors supported, and the accessibility of services to businesses. Membership alone does not guarantee immediate access or measurable reductions in transaction costs.
The next phase will focus on implementation by Ethiopia’s commercial banks and other eligible financial institutions, which must establish technical connections, meet regulatory and compliance requirements, and develop the operational capacity to process payments through the network. The pace of onboarding, the introduction of customer-facing services, and the growth of transaction volumes will determine how quickly businesses benefit. Foreign-exchange availability, regulatory differences, logistics costs, and market-access barriers will remain broader challenges that payment connectivity alone cannot resolve.
PAPSS CEO Mike Ogbalu III said Ethiopia’s participation would enable the country’s financial institutions to connect to pan-African payment infrastructure, extending the network’s reach into another important African market. However, the announcement did not include specific transaction targets, investment commitments, or estimates of potential savings, leaving the scale of the economic impact dependent on adoption and implementation.
Ethiopia is also scheduled to host PAPSS COWRY 2026, Africa’s Payments Conference, on 26–27 November at the Ethiopian Skylight Hotel in Addis Ababa. Co-hosted by PAPSS and the National Bank of Ethiopia, the event is expected to bring together banks, regulators, payment service providers, and other stakeholders to discuss cross-border payment solutions and the development of Africa’s payments ecosystem. It will provide an opportunity for Ethiopian financial institutions to engage with regional counterparts, explore partnerships, and exchange implementation experience. Its broader significance will depend on whether discussions translate into practical cooperation and wider adoption of interoperable payment systems.
Afreximbank has indicated that further expansion of PAPSS is expected before the end of 2026, potentially extending the platform’s reach to additional markets. For Ethiopia, the immediate priority is to turn formal membership into operational connectivity. Progress will depend on commercial-bank onboarding, the availability of services and supported currencies, growth in transaction activity, and demonstrable improvements in payment efficiency.
Read Also:
Ethiopia’s admission to PAPSS represents an opportunity to deepen its integration with Africa’s financial infrastructure and facilitate regional trade and investment. However, the immediate development is the creation of an additional payment pathway rather than a guarantee of instant benefits. As the country prepares to host PAPSS COWRY 2026, attention will shift towards the pace of implementation, the participation of financial institutions, and the extent to which businesses begin using the system. These factors will ultimately determine whether membership delivers measurable improvements in cross-border payments and economic integration across Africa.

Africa’s drive to turn its mineral wealth into jobs, stronger industries and improved living conditions took centre stage at the African Minerals Policy Forum, Mining in Motion 2026.
The summit focused on how countries can retain more value from their natural resources while attracting investment and protecting mining communities.
Held under the theme “One Continent, One Policy: Aligning Africa’s Mineral Future,” the gathering brought together political leaders, traditional authorities, policymakers, investors and industry players.
Discussions covered local mineral processing, mining reforms, environmental restoration and cooperation among African countries.
President Mahama targets nine sectors with $10 billion investment plan to create jobs
A central concern was how Africa could leverage growing global demand for minerals to expand its manufacturing capacity. Speakers called for investment in reliable electricity, transport, technology and skills to help countries process minerals locally and create opportunities for domestic businesses.
President John Dramani Mahama announced a target to end Ghana’s export of raw mineral ores by 2030. He said the government would support the goal with legal measures and clear implementation timelines, alongside plans to modernise the Volta Aluminium Company (VALCO) and develop domestic alumina refining.
The Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, said Cabinet had approved a revised Minerals and Mining Policy and endorsed proposed amendments to the mining law for parliamentary consideration. He said the changes would strengthen local participation, protect communities and provide investors with clearer rules.
Liberia’s Vice President called for mining development to support the wider economy through investment in electricity, transport, agriculture, manufacturing and skills. He stressed that infrastructure developed for mining should also benefit households and local businesses.
African Union Commissioner Francisca Tatchouop Belobe said Ghana’s efforts to promote local participation and mineral processing offered lessons for other African countries. She also acknowledged President Mahama’s leadership on continental financial institutions and said the forum could help shape priorities ahead of Ghana’s anticipated 2027 AU chairmanship.
On gold trade reforms, President Mahama commended GoldBod for helping to increase recorded small-scale gold exports and foreign exchange earnings.
GoldBod Chief Executive Officer Sammy Gyamfi said stronger oversight was aimed at addressing trade leakages. He cited a SWISSAID analysis that identified an estimated US$11.4 billion gap between Ghana’s reported gold exports and trading partners’ import records from 2019 to 2023.
The summit’s partnership with Investing in African Mining Indaba seeks to connect these policy priorities with international investors and financing opportunities.

articles.title: Ghana and BRICS: Strategic optionality or an expensive signal? (Part 2) - Adomonline.com
articles.summary: Ghana and BRICS: Strategic optionality or an expensive signal? (Part 2)  Adomonline.com
articles.full_text:
GEOPOLITICAL IMPLICATIONS
Ghana has historically presented itself as non-aligned, and Samuel Abu Jinapor has pressed this point.
The government’s answer is that diversification is not alignment.
In practice, Ghana is hedging on several fronts at once: it co-hosted the US military’s African Lion exercise this year, accepts West African deportees from the United States, signed a security and defence partnership with the EU and agreed a Growth Partnership with the UK that includes a £101 million shipyard at Takoradi.
At the same time it has deepened ties with China, India and Russia. Moscow’s foreign minister has publicly urged Ghana to ratify a military-technical agreement, and Russia is promoting a nuclear cooperation memorandum.
Membership of a bloc with Russia and Iran in it would make this hedge harder to present as neutral.
The United States
Washington is the most sensitive relationship. In July 2025 President Trump threatened an additional 10% tariff on countries aligning with BRICS’s “anti-American” policies, a threat made without detailed criteria.
Whether it would apply to an applicant is unknown. Two considerations cut in different directions:
Legal toolkit
The Supreme Court’s February 2026 ruling on emergency-powers tariffs arguably narrows the easiest legal route for such a surcharge, although other trade statutes remain available.
In July 2026 the US Trade Representative imposed tariffs of 10 or 12.5% on 60 economies under forced-labour rules, and Ghana was not on the list, while Nigeria, South Africa and Egypt were.
Leverage in practice
AGOA renewal, the unfinished bespoke trade deal and US Export-Import Bank financing for Ghana’s private sector are all discretionary.
Washington does not need a new tariff to make Ghana’s life harder.
US goods trade with Ghana was about US$2.5 billion in 2025, small compared with trade with the BRICS economies above, which is why supporters argue the downside is manageable.
The risk is less the dollar value of trade than its composition: the US is a key buyer of Ghanaian cocoa and a gatekeeper for AGOA-dependent manufacturing.
Inside the bloc
Joining would give Ghana a place in discussions on global trade, development finance and reform of international institutions and it would make Ghana the first West African member.
But the bloc is internally divided, decisions are by consensus and the 2027 chair is China. India’s sponsorship matters, because New Delhi chairs this year and is cautious on anything resembling an anti-Western coalition.
Even so, India cannot deliver admission alone, and the bloc already has more applicants than it has absorbed.
Markets are sceptical about speed. A Polymarket contract on any new full member joining BRICS in 2026 stood near 12.5% on 7 October, on thin volume.
That is an indicator of sentiment and not a forecast to rely on, but it fits the picture that a 2026 admission is unlikely.
Regional politics
Ghana sits between ECOWAS and the Sahel states that left it. Mahama has an envoy to the Alliance of Sahel States and hosts the AfCFTA secretariat.
BRICS membership could raise Ghana’s profile as a regional bridge or it could complicate relations with ECOWAS partners, including Nigeria, which chose partner status instead of full membership.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS
The starting point
The case is being made from a position of improved strength:
| Indicator | Latest reading | 
| Real GDP growth, 2025 | About 6% | 
| Inflation | 5.4% end-2025; 5.3% in June 2026 (IMF) | 
| Public debt | From 69.8% of GDP in 2024 to 56.6% in 2025; 54.9% projected for 2026 | 
| Current account, 2025 | Surplus of 7.9% of GDP (IMF) | 
| Gross reserves | Roughly US$12–14.5 billion depending on date and definition | 
| Ratings | Fitch B (positive), Moody’s Caa1 (positive), S&P B- | 
This is a position of strength built under an IMF programme and the Fund still flags vulnerabilities: energy-sector costs, debt-restructuring loose ends (agreements with about half of bilateral creditors under the G20 Common Framework at the time of the May review) and the fiscal cost of the domestic gold purchase programme.
Sovereign financing and market access
Ghana’s priority is to return to international capital markets on good terms and each rating upgrade matters.
A BRICS bid does not change the fundamentals, but investors may price perceived political risk, especially if it sours relations with the United States or complicates IMF engagement.
The offset is that BRICS-linked sources, such as the NDB and Gulf and Asian investors, can broaden Ghana’s financing base. The right test is whether the investor base widens or merely shifts.
The NDB: the most concrete prize
The NDB has admitted Bangladesh, the UAE, Egypt, Algeria and Uzbekistan as members, and lists Uruguay, Colombia, Ethiopia, Angola and Zimbabwe as prospective members.
Its rules let non-BRICS states join, provided the five founders keep at least 55% of voting power.
NDB leadership has said about a quarter of its lending is in local currencies of its members, with a target of 30% in 2026.
Local-currency financing would reduce foreign-exchange risk for Ghanaian infrastructure and energy projects, but a few cautions apply.
Most of the NDB’s lending remains in hard currency and mostly to sovereigns, membership requires capital subscription, and Ghana’s loan eligibility depends on credit standing like any other lenders.
The CRA and the IMF
Full membership is the only way to access the CRA. That has option value, but the CRA’s design has historically linked larger drawings to an IMF programme and it has not been a significant source of crisis lending in practice.
Ghana is also under an IMF PCI that expects fiscal discipline. Treating the CRA as an alternative to the IMF would be premature, and officials have said they are not doing so.
Payments and the dollar
The practical action is already under way. The Bank of Ghana says importers can now pay for Chinese goods from cedi accounts under a pilot that routes through China’s CIPS payment system, with the dollar and SWIFT still available.
Benefits are real: lower conversion costs for small and mid-sized importers and less dollar demand at the margin.
Limits are real too. China sells Ghana far more than it buys, so Ghana needs a steady supply of yuan, and the cedi-yuan market lacks depth. Gold and cocoa remain priced in dollars.
And BRICS payment work is incremental plumbing, not an alternative reserve asset.
The bank-level opportunity is similar for rupee and rand corridors, given India and South Africa’s weight in Ghana’s trade.
Banks and compliance
For Ghana’s banking sector, the most under-discussed issue is correspondent banking. Ghanaian banks depend on US-dollar clearing and on large international correspondents.
Membership in a bloc that includes sanctioned jurisdictions could raise compliance scrutiny, de-risking or higher costs, even though nothing in BRICS membership itself breaches sanctions.
This is a risk assessment, not a reported event, but it is a reasonable question for the Bank of Ghana and the Ghana Association of Banks to put to the government.
Conversely, new corridors could create fee income, trade-finance products and cross-border lending lines. Net effects depend on how carefully banks manage sanctions exposure.
Scenarios
| Scenario | What it looks like | Implications | 
| Partner-country route | Ghana is admitted as a partner or joins the NDB first | Captures most financial and diplomatic upside at low cost; avoids the most contentious votes | 
| Full membership, slow | Admission in 2027 or later after consensus | Gains a seat and CRA access; Ghana must manage US reaction, AGOA and market perception | 
| Application stalls | Members defer or ask Ghana to wait | Limited direct cost, but it may have strained relations with Washington for little return | 
| Washington retaliates | Trade preferences or financing become harder | Cocoa, garments and private-sector credit take the hit; strengthens critics of the move | 
4. What a sensible approach would look like
Publish the cost-benefit analysis and brief Parliament, as the Minority has requested. A decision of this weight should rest on a documented case, including financing terms and obligations.
Sequence the moves. Settle AGOA and the bespoke US trade arrangement before the application becomes formal, or at least before any final admission.
Consider partner status and NDB membership first. These capture much of the financial upside and keep full membership as an option.
Set specific asks. Examples include local-currency financing lines, pharmaceutical and vaccine manufacturing investment, rail projects, and market access for processed goods, not just raw commodities.
Protect the IMF and Western relationships. Make clear in word and deed that the PCI, World Bank engagement and EU, UK and US ties continue.
Prepare the banking system. Give banks guidance on cedi-yuan, rupee and rand corridors, and engage correspondent banks early on sanctions-compliance expectations.
Avoid foreign-policy positions in declarations that are not in Ghana’s interest. Use consensus rules to stay out of contested statements on Iran, Ukraine and Gaza-related issues.
Track outcomes. Define metrics (processed-goods exports, local-currency lending, cedi-settled trade, spreads on sovereign debt) and report on them annually.
5. Bottom line
Ghana’s interest in BRICS is a rational response to a world in which trade, aid and finance have become more conditional.
The government is right that Ghana’s commercial reality already points toward India, China, the Gulf and South Africa.
But the benefits most worth having (local-currency finance, cheaper payments, industrial partnerships) are available without a full commitment, while the costs (US reaction, sanctions exposure, investor perception) fall on a country still rebuilding credibility after default.
The case for applying is stronger as an option to be exercised carefully than as an immediate piv

articles.title: Ethiopia's FDI surges 49% to $1.43 billion as forex reforms and special economic zones take hold - Businessfront
articles.summary: Ethiopia's FDI surges 49% to $1.43 billion as forex reforms and special economic zones take hold  Businessfront
articles.full_text:
Ethiopia attracted $1.43 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI) in the first quarter of its 2026/27 fiscal year, a 49% jump year-on-year, as a market-based foreign exchange system and expanded special economic zones begin to reshape the country’s investment landscape.
The Ethiopian Investment Commission (EIC) — the federal body responsible for promoting and facilitating investment into the country — released the figures on 20 October following its quarterly performance review.
The inflows exceeded the government’s quarterly target of $900 million by $532 million, representing approximately 159% of the planned amount.
Based on the reported annual growth rate, FDI in the corresponding quarter of the 2025/26 fiscal year stood at approximately $961 million, placing the scale of the year-on-year increase in sharper relief.
The EIC also issued 179 new investment licences during the quarter against a target of 123 — a 46% overshoot — with the total number of licences rising 45.5% compared with the same period a year earlier. Of the newly licensed investments, 122 were registered outside special economic zones, while 57 were located within the designated zones.
Activity within special economic zones and free trade zones expanded markedly. The commission signed 110 agreements during the quarter against a target of 50, representing 220% of the quarterly plan.
The EIC did not disclose the combined investment value of those agreements or provide a breakdown by sector or country of origin.
The results reflect, in part, a significant policy shift introduced in July 2024, when the National Bank of Ethiopia — the country’s central bank — moved to a market-based foreign exchange system as part of a broader economic reform programme aimed at addressing chronic foreign currency shortages and improving the operating environment for businesses.
The government has simultaneously pursued the development of special economic zones to attract investment in manufacturing, processing, and export-oriented industries.
Beyond new approvals, the commission reported progress in converting registered projects into operational activity.
During the quarter, 81 investment projects entered the implementation stage and 66 reached the production phase — both above their respective quarterly targets, though the EIC did not disclose the planned figures or the capital deployed in those projects.
The distinction matters: newly issued licences and signed agreements do not necessarily represent capital already deployed or production capacity brought online.
The commission did not specify how much of the $1.43 billion came from new investments, expansion projects, or reinvested earnings, nor did it provide a sectoral breakdown of the total FDI figure.
Export revenue associated with the commission’s quarterly performance reached $238 million, exceeding its target, though the EIC did not identify which sectors accounted for the earnings. Investment activities also generated more than 22,000 new employment opportunities during the reporting period.
Meleket Sahlu, deputy commissioner of the EIC, attributed the quarterly results to measures aimed at addressing operational constraints, strengthening investor support, facilitating business expansion, and encouraging the reinvestment of earnings.
Speaking during the performance review, Meleket said the commission would continue addressing implementation gaps identified in the quarterly assessment.
The EIC has not yet disclosed its full-year FDI target or the geographic and sectoral composition of the first-quarter inflows, leaving a fuller picture of where capital is flowing — and from whom — still to emerge.

articles.title: Egyptian Fintech MNT-Halan Raises $150 Million in IPO as Shares Surge 18% on Trading Debut - Tech In Africa
articles.summary: Egyptian Fintech MNT-Halan Raises $150 Million in IPO as Shares Surge 18% on Trading Debut  Tech In Africa
articles.full_text:
Egyptian fintech company MNT-Halan has made a strong debut on the Egyptian Exchange following an initial public offering (IPO) that raised EGP 7.84 billion, approximately $150 million, attracting significant interest from local and international investors.
The company’s shares climbed as much as 18% during their first trading session on October 20, 2026, rising from the offering price of EGP 24.50 to EGP 28.91. The increase valued its listed Egyptian operations at approximately $745 million.
The IPO involved the sale of 320 million existing shares, representing 20% of MNT Tech Holding for Financial Investments, by its parent company, MNT Investments B.V.
Investor demand significantly exceeded the available shares, with the institutional tranche subscribed 11.2 times and the retail offering oversubscribed 43.6 times.
The transaction attracted more than 41,500 retail orders and participation from over 300 institutional investors across at least 10 countries.
Among the major investors were Commercial International Bank, one of Egypt’s leading private-sector banks, and London-based investment manager Redwheel.
Both institutions participated as cornerstone investors, collectively committing to more than one-third of the initial offering.
Investment banking firm EFG Hermes served as joint global coordinator and joint bookrunner for the transaction.
Founded in 2018, MNT-Halan provides financial services, including microfinance, consumer lending and financing for small businesses. Its operations combine digital technology with a network of more than 1,200 physical distribution points across Egypt.
By June 2026, the company’s Egyptian business reported approximately 1.9 million active customers and a gross loan portfolio worth EGP 46.7 billion.
For 2025, it recorded adjusted revenue of EGP 20.5 billion and net income of EGP 1.98 billion, representing a 44% annual increase in profit.
MNT-Halan’s parent company plans to reinvest up to EGP 4 billion from the offering proceeds into its Egyptian operations to support future expansion.
The successful listing represents a significant development for Egypt’s capital markets, marking the country’s largest IPO by dollar value since 2021.
It also provides a potential benchmark for other Egyptian technology companies considering public listings, although future investor confidence will depend on sustained financial performance and broader economic stability.

Stockholm [Sweden], October 21: EU-India Free Trade Agreement: Boosting Trade and Growth, a recent report prepared by the Confederation of Swedish Enterprise in close cooperation with CII estimates that the agreement could increase India-EU trade by up to US$133.9 billion by 2035. The event organised by India Unlimited, brought together over 350 participants, alongside senior government representatives, a high-level Haryana delegation, representatives of the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), business leaders, investors and innovators. Held under the theme "India-Sweden 2035: Innovation for a Competitive Future," the event centered on the India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) and its potential to expand trade, encourage investment and deepen industrial and technology partnerships between India and Sweden.
Held in Stockholm on 15th October, 2026, the event featured inaugural addresses by Shri Nayab Singh, Hon'ble Chief Minister of Haryana, Mr. Benjamin Dousa, Hon'ble Minister for International Development Cooperation and Foreign Trade, Government of Sweden, Mr. Jan-Olof Jacke, Director General, Confederation of Swedish Enterprise, H.E. Anurag Bhushan, Ambassador of India to Sweden, Government of India and Robin Sukhia, Secretary General and CEO, Sweden-India Business Council. The inaugural session focused on strengthening the India-Sweden partnership and translating shared ambitions into practical collaboration, investment and market opportunities.
Shri Nayab Singh, Hon'ble Chief Minister of Haryana, in his inaugural address, said, "India-Sweden Innovation Day provides an important platform to strengthen cooperation in technology, innovation and manufacturing. Bilateral trade has grown from US 7.75 billion in 2025, and our countries share the ambition of doubling economic exchanges, including trade and investment, over the next five years. Haryana is keen to contribute to this growth through deeper partnerships under 'Make in India' and 'Made with Sweden'. articles.title: Ethiopia Runs 3.2 Billion US Dollars Trade Deficit with UAE in Five Years - Birr Metrics
articles.summary: Ethiopia Runs 3.2 Billion US Dollars Trade Deficit with UAE in Five Years  Birr Metrics
articles.full_text:
Imports account for nearly four-fifths of bilateral trade as Ethiopian officials seek Emirati investment in local manufacturing.
Ethiopia accumulated a merchandise trade deficit of 3.2 billion US dollars with the United Arab Emirates between 2021 and 2025, as imports from the Gulf country exceeded Ethiopian exports by more than threefold, according to figures disclosed by the Ministry of Trade and Regional Integration.
Bilateral trade reached 5.6 billion US dollars during the five-year period, comprising 4.4 billion US dollars in imports and 1.2 billion US dollars in exports, a ministry representative told the Ethiopia–UAE Business and Investment Forum in Addis Ababa on October 20.
Imports accounted for 78.6 percent of the bilateral merchandise trade reported for the period. For every US dollar Ethiopia earned from exports to the UAE, it spent approximately 3.67 US dollars on imports from the country.
Petroleum products accounted for the largest share of imports, followed by urea fertiliser. Coffee led Ethiopian exports, followed by sesame, meat products, cut flowers and fresh produce.
The figures illustrate the composition of trade with a major Gulf partner. Ethiopia imports petroleum products and fertiliser, both important inputs for domestic economic activity, while its exports are concentrated in agricultural commodities and related products.
The ministry did not release an annual breakdown showing whether the deficit widened or narrowed over the five-year period. The reported totals also do not establish how much merchandise originated in the UAE rather than passing through its trading and logistics networks.
The disclosure coincided with a visit by a Sharjah business delegation exploring manufacturing, agribusiness and commercial partnerships in Ethiopia. The Sharjah Chamber of Commerce and Industry organised the October 19–22 mission through its export development centre.
Ethiopian officials encouraged the delegation to consider local production, technology transfer and job creation, rather than concentrating solely on the import and distribution of goods. Areas identified for potential cooperation included agro-processing, textiles, pharmaceuticals, construction materials and packaging.
The government has sought to strengthen export earnings, expand manufacturing and attract investment alongside macroeconomic reforms, including changes to the foreign exchange regime introduced in July 2024. New factories could replace some imported goods or produce for export, although initial construction and equipment purchases can themselves increase imports.
The delegation’s programme included meetings with government agencies and private businesses. Officials did not announce a value for new investment commitments, specific factory projects or binding financing agreements at the forum.

articles.title: Ramaphosa warns South Africa to prepare for loss of US-Africa trade deal - IOL
articles.summary: Ramaphosa warns South Africa to prepare for loss of US-Africa trade deal  IOL
articles.full_text:
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the country should "prepare" for the possibility of being removed from Washington's duty-free trade programme for Africa, as ties between the two nations continue to fray.
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which grants eligible sub-Saharan African countries preferential access to the US market, has been renewed until the end of 2028.
South Africa is the scheme's largest beneficiary, but its eligibility has come under scrutiny as Washington steps up criticism of Pretoria, including false allegations of discrimination against white Afrikaners that South Africa rejects.
"Congress has decided that we should be kept in AGOA. What now remains is the executive," Ramaphosa said, referring to the pact now needing President Donald Trump's signature after approval by Congress.
"And by the way, so that I prepare our people for this, if we ever have a choice, we are not the first and only country to be taken out of AGOA. And I believe we will not be the last," he said in response to a question from an AFP journalist during a briefing.
Bilateral ties have deteriorated since Trump took office, with Washington cutting aid, expelling South Africa's ambassador and berating Ramaphosa in the Oval Office over discredited claims of a "white genocide".
Washington in mid-September announced restrictions on visas for South Africans who promote "race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa" – all issues that are disputed between the two countries.
Last year, the US launched a programme to resettle white Afrikaners who say they face persecution and violent crime in South Africa.
By September 30, the US had admitted 16 287 South Africans under the programme over the preceding year. They were the only people granted refugee status by Washington during that period, apart from five Afghans.
'Devastating' impact
The US president reviews countries' eligibility for AGOA annually.
Any removal requires 60 days' notice to Congress and the country concerned. To take effect on 1 January, an exclusion must be announced by 2 November.
Former president Joe Biden declared the Central African Republic, Gabon, Niger and Uganda ineligible on 30 October, 2023, with the exclusions taking effect on 1 January, 2024.
South Africa is going to look for alternative markets to minimise the impacts of such an exclusion, Ramaphosa said.
"I need as president to prepare us if it ever happens. So we should not go out and jump off tall buildings and think that this is the end of the world," he said, conceding that the impacts would nonetheless be "devastating".
Within AGOA, Washington exempts South African cars from customs duties.
After precious metals, cars are the country's second-biggest export earner to the US, according to the South African tax authorities.
In 2025, the automobile employers' organisation Naamsa said 86 000 jobs were directly tied to the accord at car manufacturers, a number that increases to 125 000 when including their sub-contractors.
