articles.title: Africa seeks closer BRI cooperation in trade, financing - China Daily Global Edition
articles.summary: Africa seeks closer BRI cooperation in trade, financing  China Daily Global Edition
articles.full_text:
By VICTOR RABALLA in Nairobi, Kenya | China Daily | Updated: 2026-10-22 09:36
China and African countries are seeking closer cooperation in infrastructure, trade and financing to strengthen regional connectivity, expand local industries and support economic growth, representatives said at the Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum 2026 on Wednesday.
Speaking in Nairobi, Chinese Ambassador to Kenya Guo Haiyan stressed China's commitment to align Belt and Road cooperation with Africa's development priorities.
Guo pledged deeper financial cooperation that would help ease investment constraints and advance projects that benefit communities across the continent.
"We will closely align Belt and Road cooperation with the AU's Agenda 2063," she said, referring to the African Union's long-term development blueprint.
Guo said China would support African countries in pursuing modernization suited to their national circumstances, while expanding trade cooperation and helping local producers capture more value from their products.
The forum, held simultaneously in Beijing and Nairobi, was organized by the Export-Import Bank of China.
Chen Huaiyu, chairman of the Export-Import Bank of China, said the bank would deepen cooperation in railways, ports and energy, while expanding partnerships with financial institutions to support development in countries engaged with BRI.
Over more than a decade, the bank had extended more than 7 trillion yuan ($1.05 trillion) in cumulative Belt and Road loans, with operations covering more than 130 participating countries, he said at the forum in Beijing.
Chen said that future support would target clean energy, the digital economy, agriculture and industrial cooperation, helping partner countries build local industries and strengthen their capacity for independent development.
He said more diverse financing arrangements would help partner countries improve their financing structures while balancing development needs with debt sustainability.
In Kenya, plans to extend the Mombasa-Nairobi standard gauge railway, or SGR, to Kisumu, in western Kenya, illustrate how better transport connections could expand the benefits of infrastructure investment.
Philip Mainga, Kenya Railways Corporation managing director, said that construction of the extension had begun, with completion expected in two years.
"We expect the first phase of the project, extending to Kisumu, to be completed within two years," he said.
Reaching Kisumu would connect the railway to Lake Victoria, opening opportunities to serve regional markets and strengthen the movement of goods through the Port of Mombasa on the coast of the Indian Ocean.
Mainga identified Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, South Sudan and Rwanda among the countries expected to benefit from stronger regional transport links.
"The extension would help attract more regional cargo through Mombasa and provide an additional route for exports moving from inland production centers to overseas markets, including China", he said.
He said avocados, coffee and tea were among the products that could benefit from greater use of rail freight, noting that much of this cargo currently travels by road.
Kenya's Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi told the Nairobi forum that investment in transport, energy, water and information and communication technology was central to the country's development agenda.
He described the Belt and Road Initiative as an important framework for improving connectivity, expanding trade and widening access to development finance.
Lesotho's Finance Minister Retselisitsoe Adelaide Matlanyane stressed the need for affordable, predictable financing aligned with national development plans and delivering measurable benefits to communities. She said efforts to attract international capital should go hand in hand with expanding access to financial services at home.
"Open finance is not just about cross-border flows, it is about opening systems to our own citizens," she said in Beijing, citing mobile money's contribution to financial inclusion in Lesotho.

articles.title: Nigeria’s carbon market gains momentum as Africa urged to deliver projects - Daily Trust
articles.summary: Nigeria’s carbon market gains momentum as Africa urged to deliver projects  Daily Trust
articles.full_text:
Nigeria’s carbon market is gaining traction following the Federal Government’s first approvals for international carbon credit sales, a Nigerian carbon project developer, 9JA Carbon Trade, has said.
The company said the approvals demonstrated that Nigeria’s carbon market framework was operational, as African governments, investors and project developers were urged to move beyond developing regulations to delivering projects and securing investment.
The position was made known after 9JA Carbon Trade participated in the Carbon Markets Africa Summit (CMAS) 2026, held in Kigali, Rwanda, from October 14 to 15.
The summit attracted about 600 delegates from 52 countries, representing more than 150 organisations, including over 50 investors and buyers.
Speaking at the event, Timothy Solomon, Co-Technical Manager of 9JA Carbon Trade, said Africa’s carbon market was increasingly being judged by its ability to deliver credible carbon credits, attract investment and ensure that host communities benefited from projects.
“Kigali changed the question Africa is asked. It is no longer whether the continent can supply carbon credits, but whether it can deliver them with integrity, at fair prices and with benefits host communities can see,” Solomon said.
“ Nigeria now has the framework and its first approvals. Our part is to bring forward projects worth approving,” he added.
At a session on country readiness on October 14, Ibrahim Shelleng, Senior Special Assistant to the President on Climate Finance and Stakeholder Engagement, disclosed that Nigeria issued six letters of authorisation in March 2026 and two additional letters by September.
A letter of authorisation is a formal government approval allowing carbon credits to be used internationally. Under the arrangement, the host country agrees not to count the authorised emission reductions towards its own climate targets.
Reacting to the development, Ekene Okpara, also a Co-Technical Manager at 9JA Carbon Trade, said Nigeria’s progress in issuing authorisations gave developers confidence in the country’s approval process.
Okpara, however, sought clarification on whether the Federal Government planned to enter into a bilateral carbon agreement with another country.
He also asked what guidance was available for developers whose projects were still awaiting approval from the National Council on Climate Change, the body responsible for approving carbon projects in Nigeria.
On October 15, the company participated in a round-table discussion at the summit’s solution lab, which examined ways to reduce risks for private investors, including political risks, insurance, financing and access to carbon credit buyers.
The discussions formed part of broader efforts to strengthen Africa’s capacity to attract private capital into carbon markets and translate climate commitments into viable projects.
At the close of the summit, the Acting Permanent Secretary of Rwanda’s Ministry of Environment, speaking on behalf of the Minister of Environment, outlined six areas of agreement among participants.
The priorities included strengthening market integrity, building trust, ensuring that host communities benefited from carbon projects, increasing Africa’s share of the value generated by the market, improving regulatory implementation and securing long-term investment.
Governments were urged to complete and implement their carbon market regulations and publish information on authorisations and credit transfers to improve transparency.
Buyers and investors were also encouraged to move beyond expressing interest in African carbon credits and sign multi-year purchase agreements at fair prices.
Development partners and financial institutions were called upon to support project preparation, identified at the summit as a major obstacle preventing viable projects from reaching the market.
Opening the summit on October 14, Rwanda’s Minister of Environment, Dr Bernadette Arakwiye, said developing regulations alone was insufficient without effective implementation.
“Writing rules is one thing, and running them is another,” she said.
Arakwiye noted that improved cookstoves accounted for approximately 87 per cent of Rwanda’s issued carbon credits, while agriculture had generated barely one per cent of voluntary carbon market credits over two decades.
The summit also examined emerging international demand for carbon credits and the growing importance of quality standards in determining their market value.
The International Air Transport Association told delegates that the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), a United Nations-backed scheme for international aviation, would become mandatory for airlines in 2027. Credits used under the scheme must carry a government letter of authorisation.
Lukas Visek of the European Commission said a Commission proposal envisaged European Union purchases of carbon credits covering up to 260 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent between 2036 and 2040.
Participants were also told that higher-quality credits were attracting better prices.
Lorna Ritchie of the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market said credits bearing its Core Carbon Principles label sold for about 25 per cent more on average than unlabelled credits.
Meanwhile, carbon ratings agency BeZero Carbon said reforestation credits ranged from $5 to more than $40, depending on their ratings.
The summit also highlighted gaps in Africa’s carbon market infrastructure, particularly the continent’s dependence on external verification services.
The African Union Development Agency-New Partnership for Africa’s Development (AUDA-NEPAD) told participants that more than 90 per cent of carbon project verification work in Africa was still handled by organisations based outside the continent, contributing to delays affecting projects.
The agency said its accelerator programme would support the development of African validation and verification bodies to strengthen local expertise and reduce dependence on external providers.
The Africa Carbon Investment and Finance Alliance (ACIFA) was also launched at the summit to establish a platform connecting carbon projects with financing opportunities. The alliance is expected to report on its progress at the next edition of the summit.
The United Nations Development Programme outlined five areas of support for carbon market development, including building investment pipelines and reducing project risks before carbon revenues become available.
As the summit concluded, participants were urged to present a unified African position at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), scheduled for November 2026, backed by evidence of progress in project delivery.
Maxwell Gomera, UNDP Resident Representative in South Africa, challenged delegates to identify concrete actions they could advance after the summit.
“Give it a name and a date,” he said.

articles.title: Ruto to hand over COMESA chairmanship to Mnangagwa - The Star, Kenya
articles.summary: Ruto to hand over COMESA chairmanship to Mnangagwa  The Star, Kenya
articles.full_text:
President William Ruto has arrived in Harare, Zimbabwe, ahead of the 25th Summit of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) Heads of State and Government, where he is expected to hand over the bloc’s chairmanship to Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa on Thursday.
Ruto arrived at Robert Gabriel Mugabe International Airport on Wednesday evening to join other heads of state and government for the summit.
He was received by Tourism and Hospitality Industry Minister Barbara Rwodzi and other senior government officials.
Ruto said the summit will focus on deepening regional integration, strengthening peace and security, accelerating implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), advancing industrialisation and unlocking the economic potential of Africa’s natural resources through value addition.
The handover will mark the end of Kenya’s tenure at the helm of the regional economic bloc after Ruto took over the chairmanship in 2025 from Burundi’s President Évariste Ndayishimiye.
The summit brings together leaders from the 21-member bloc to deliberate on regional trade, industrialisation, investment and economic integration.
This year’s meeting is being held under the theme, “One Market, One Future: Advancing Inclusive Industrialisation, Investment and Regional Integration in COMESA.”
The leaders are expected to review progress in implementing the bloc’s economic integration agenda and explore ways of strengthening trade among member states.
COMESA seeks to promote economic prosperity through regional integration, trade liberalisation and cooperation among member states.
The bloc provides a platform for countries to coordinate policies aimed at easing cross-border trade, expanding markets for local producers and attracting investment.
Kenya has been pursuing expanded regional markets as part of efforts to grow exports, create jobs and strengthen commercial ties with neighbouring countries.
Kenya's Ambassador to Zimbabwe Gertrude Angote said Wednesday that Kenya is looking forward to strengthening regional ties and advancing COMESA’s continental objectives as Ruto prepares to hand over the chairmanship.
Ruto’s tenure has placed Kenya at the centre of discussions on regional economic cooperation, with the summit providing an opportunity for member states to assess progress and set priorities for the next phase of integration.
The transition to Zimbabwe’s leadership comes as African countries intensify efforts to boost intra-African trade under the AfCFTA, which seeks to establish a single market for goods and services across the continent.
Regional integration remains a key priority for economies seeking to reduce trade barriers, strengthen manufacturing and improve the movement of goods across national borders.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday called on US President Donald Trump to invite South Africa to the G20 summit in Miami in December.
Speaking at the Berlin Global Dialogue conference, Merz said anyone discussing the global economy's future must involve all major partners. "Obviously, Africa belongs at the table," he stressed.
"The African Union is a member of the G20. And so is South Africa. That's why I urge that South Africa be represented at the G20 summit," the chancellor said, referring to the summit of the world's major industrial and emerging economies.
Trump earlier announced that South Africa would not receive an invitation to the 2026 summit. The decision followed Washington's boycott of the Johannesburg summit and stemmed from Trump's claims of persecution against white farmers in South Africa.
In his speech, Merz said the G20 remains a key platform for economic cooperation and global prosperity, and argued that Europe, as the world's largest single market, should have a greater say in the group.
He thanked Trump for inviting EU members Spain, the Netherlands and Poland to take part as guests alongside regular members. "I will work to ensure that they remain part of the G20 loop in future," he added.
Merz said this year's G20 summit should focus on issues vital for the future of the world economy, including the opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence, a secure and affordable energy supply, how to address unfair trade practices, and rising public debt worldwide.
He also suggested prioritizing discussions on growth at the G20 summit in Miami. "Because today more than ever, economic stability and prosperity depend on the international environment," he said. "To this end, we have proposed the Miami growth agenda to the US. We want to cut red tape jointly, drive necessary structural reforms and facilitate investment."

The programme includes investment pitch sessions for pre-screened companies seeking capital, alongside discussions on energy infrastructure, digital systems, hospitality real estate and agribusiness.
Participants will examine modular energy solutions for tourism and hospitality businesses, as well as opportunities in fintech, digital trade facilitation and other emerging technologies.
The real estate discussions will explore investment opportunities in hotels, short-term rentals, ecotourism and nature-based developments.
Agribusiness and agro-processing will also feature prominently, with sessions examining commodity markets, supply chain integration and opportunities to link agriculture with tourism.
Prof Gabriel Eshun is expected to lead discussions on agribusiness, agro-processing and agrotourism investment.

The event will culminate in a beach networking gala at Lush on the Coast in Cape Coast, bringing together delegates, sponsors, government officials and diplomatic representatives.

articles.title: Zimplow Swings to US$891,000 Profit as Mining Demand Rises - The Zimbabwe Mail
articles.summary: Zimplow Swings to US$891,000 Profit as Mining Demand Rises  The Zimbabwe Mail
articles.full_text:
HARARE – Zimbabwean industrial equipment group Zimplow Holdings Limited has returned to profitability, reporting a US$891,063 pre-tax profit for the nine months ended September 2026, as stronger agricultural machinery sales, growing demand from the mining industry and improved cost management helped reverse losses recorded a year earlier.
The result represents a US$1.54 million turnaround from the US$650,998 pre-tax loss reported during the corresponding period in 2025, providing evidence that the group’s restructuring and diversification strategy is beginning to strengthen its earnings.
According to a trading update dated 15 October 2026, seen by The Zimbabwe Mail business desk, group revenue increased 10.6 percent to US$24.88 million from US$22.49 million, while the gross profit margin improved to 28.2 percent from 26.3 percent.
The improvement suggests that Zimplow is generating stronger returns from its sales while benefiting from changes to its operating structure introduced over the past year.
A particularly encouraging development was the acceleration in profitability during the third quarter.
The company generated US$634,775 in pre-tax profit between July and September, compared with US$256,288 earned during the entire first half of the year.
The third quarter consequently accounted for approximately 71 percent of the group’s nine-month pre-tax earnings, highlighting a significant improvement in operating momentum.
The company attributed the stronger performance to improved stock availability, increased economic activity and the benefits of adjustments to its cost base and business model.
Farmec leads recovery as agricultural equipment sales strengthen
Farmec, Zimplow’s agricultural machinery distribution business, remained the largest contributor to group profitability.
Revenue increased 25.7 percent to US$10.11 million, while pre-tax profit rose 151.9 percent to US$565,297.
Tractor sales increased 14 percent to 122 units, while agricultural implement sales rose 23.8 percent to 369 units.
The business also recorded a 24.6 percent increase in spare parts revenue to US$1.73 million, reflecting continued demand for equipment maintenance and replacement components.
Workshop activity increased 20 percent to 9,218 hours, although service revenue declined marginally by 1.6 percent to US$653,237.
The figures suggest that Farmec’s recovery has been supported by both new equipment sales and recurring aftermarket demand, an important consideration for businesses operating in cyclical agricultural markets.
Zimplow said the division had focused on strengthening product support, improving supply-chain efficiency and securing attractive supplier credit arrangements.
Access to supplier financing is particularly important for equipment distributors because it can reduce pressure on working capital while allowing businesses to maintain adequate inventories.
Scanlink profits surge despite weaker revenue
The group’s commercial vehicle business, Scanlink, delivered one of the strongest improvements in profitability despite a slight decline in turnover.
Revenue eased 1.1 percent to US$5.31 million, but pre-tax profit increased 212 percent to US$402,218.
Truck sales more than tripled to 34 units, while bus sales declined 20 percent to 16 units.
The division benefited from increased direct customer sales and stronger aftermarket activity.
Spare parts revenue rose 30.7 percent to US$2.47 million, while service revenue increased 15.3 percent to US$1.04 million.
These developments helped lift Scanlink’s gross profit margin by 7.2 percentage points to 27.9 percent.
The results illustrate the financial importance of aftermarket services, which can provide recurring income and improve margins even when overall equipment sales remain uneven.
For Zimplow, the performance also demonstrates the value of maintaining a diversified revenue base across equipment distribution, spare parts and technical support.
Mining demand drives Trentyre recovery
Trentyre, the group’s tyre distribution and retreading operation, recorded a 29.8 percent increase in revenue to US$2.18 million, supported by stronger demand for new tyres from mining and agricultural customers.
New tyre revenue surged 66.7 percent to US$1.43 million, while sales volumes of off-the-road and agricultural tyres increased 66.8 percent to 522 units.
The growth was largely attributed to orders from the mining industry, which continues to provide opportunities for suppliers of industrial equipment and consumables.
Retreading revenue, however, declined 13.6 percent to US$445,108 following supply-chain disruptions earlier in the year.
Despite these challenges, the division’s gross margin improved by 5.1 percentage points to 30.8 percent.
Its pre-tax loss narrowed by 95.7 percent to just US$12,027, placing the business close to breaking even.
The performance is significant because mining-related demand provides Zimplow with an alternative source of revenue when agricultural investment weakens.
Mealie Brand expands exports to reduce drought exposure
Agricultural implement manufacturer Mealie Brand also returned to profitability, reporting pre-tax earnings of US$96,321 compared with a loss of US$43,347 a year earlier.
Revenue increased 16.1 percent to US$3.43 million, supported by export growth and the company’s expansion into mining-related products.
Export revenue rose 42.8 percent to US$1.15 million, with export implement volumes increasing 46.4 percent to 9,461 units.
Revenue from the mining segment reached US$459,843, representing 13.4 percent of the division’s turnover, despite the business having no comparable mining sales in 2025.
The expansion helped offset weaker domestic agricultural demand.
Local revenue declined 15.4 percent to US$1.81 million, while domestic implement sales volumes fell 33.9 percent to 7,150 units.
The contrasting performance highlights a central feature of Zimplow’s restructuring strategy: reducing dependence on Zimbabwe’s agricultural cycle by developing export markets and supplying equipment to other productive sectors.
For investors, this diversification could become increasingly important as changing rainfall patterns and drought risks create greater uncertainty around agricultural capital expenditure.
Solar equipment sales double as Powermec returns to profit
Powermec, the group’s power equipment business, recorded a US$30,362 pre-tax profit, reversing a US$65,334 loss in the corresponding period last year.
Revenue increased 10 percent to US$2.75 million, supported by rapid growth in solar equipment and accessories.
Solar-related revenue increased 118.7 percent to US$604,852, accounting for 22 percent of the division’s total sales.
The growth suggests that renewable energy equipment is becoming a more important part of Powermec’s business model as industrial and commercial customers consider alternative electricity supply arrangements.
Demand for conventional generators remained subdued.
Generator sales declined 32.1 percent to 36 units, while generator hire revenue fell 40.8 percent to US$80,513.
Zimplow attributed the weakness partly to relatively stable grid electricity supplies to industry during much of the reporting period.
The changing sales mix may provide opportunities for Powermec to expand its participation in distributed energy solutions, although the division’s profitability will depend on maintaining margins and controlling inventory costs.
Meanwhile, C.T. Bolts reported revenue growth of 5.3 percent to US$964,333 and returned to profitability with pre-tax earnings of US$63,798, compared with a US$761 loss previously.
The improvement was supported by a 16.8 percent reduction in operating expenses, despite continued price competition from imported fasteners.
Stronger margins point to benefits from restructuring
An analysis of the financial figures by The Zimbabwe Mail indicates that Zimplow’s recovery has been driven by more than revenue growth alone.
While turnover increased by 10.6 percent, gross profit expanded at a faster rate because the group improved its gross margin by 1.9 percentage points.
Based on the reported figures, gross profit increased from approximately US$5.91 million in the comparable nine-month period to US$7.02 million in 2026.
That represents an increase of approximately US$1.11 million, or nearly 19 percent.
The group’s pre-tax profit margin also improved to approximately 3.6 percent, compared with a negative margin of 2.9 percent a year earlier.
These figures suggest that improved pricing, a more favourable product mix and cost restructuring have strengthened the group’s ability to convert revenue into earnings.
Nevertheless, a pre-tax margin of 3.6 percent remains relatively modest, leaving profitability sensitive to changes in equipment demand, imported input costs and operating expenses.
The sustainability of the turnaround will therefore depend on Zimplow’s ability to preserve margins while expanding sales in sectors less exposed to agricultural volatility.
El Niño threatens agricultural demand in 2027
Despite the improved earnings, Zimplow warned that the outlook for the 2026/27 agricultural season remains uncertain.
The company cited forecasts pointing to below-normal rainfall and the possibility of a strong El Niño weather pattern, which could undermine agricultural production and reduce farmers’ capacity to purchase equipment.
The trading update also noted that Zimbabwe’s record tobacco output had not translated into proportionately stronger purchasing power for growers.
Although tobacco sales exceeded 357 million kilogrammes during the 2026 marketing season, the average selling price declined from US$3.30 to US$2.49 per kilogramme.

articles.title: Gulf Port Giants Invest Billions in Africa as Red Sea Shifts - Africa M.E.
articles.summary: Gulf Port Giants Invest Billions in Africa as Red Sea Shifts  Africa M.E.
articles.full_text:
A Crisis That Became a Catalyst
Three years after Houthi attacks on commercial shipping triggered a mass rerouting of vessels away from the Red Sea, the scale of the structural change is becoming measurable. According to data from BIMCO cited by Trade Finance Global, container ship transits through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal fell by more than 60% from their 2023 levels. The vessels that chose the Cape of Good Hope route added roughly one to two weeks of voyage time and approximately one million dollars in extra fuel costs per trip. Daily commercial vessel traffic around the Cape averaged 20 ships between March and late April 2026, up from just six in 2023, according to IMF data cited in ACCA’s AB Magazine.
For Egypt, the impact was direct and severe. Suez Canal revenues, a critical source of foreign exchange, collapsed as traffic dried up. For ports along Africa’s southern and eastern coastlines, the sudden surge in vessel calls exposed structural bottlenecks that existing capacity could not absorb.
A partial normalization is now underway. Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd, and MSC have each announced that select services will return to Red Sea transits as security conditions partially stabilize. The Suez Canal Authority recorded a 54% year-on-year rise in net tonnage for the first eight months of 2026. But as Ecofin Agency reported in October 2026, Lloyd’s List Intelligence counted just 184 container-ship transits through Suez in August 2026, against 549 in August 2023. The crisis lasted long enough to redirect investment capital into African port infrastructure at a pace that will outlast the security situation that triggered it.
Gulf Operators Lock In Long-Term Positions Across African Ports
DP World, the Dubai state-linked logistics operator, launched a direct shipping route between Jebel Ali and Berbera in Somaliland in October 2025. Operating on a nine-day cycle with stops at Aden and Djibouti, the service connects the UAE’s flagship hub directly to the Gulf of Aden and opens a faster corridor into landlocked Ethiopia, an economy of more than 130 million people. Beyond East Africa, DP World is developing a deep-sea port at Ndayane in Senegal and a major terminal at Banana in the Democratic Republic of Congo, as part of a commitment to invest three billion dollars in African port and logistics infrastructure over the next three to five years, according to Trade Finance Global.
Abu Dhabi’s AD Ports Group is building its African portfolio through a parallel strategy. The group secured an 81% ownership stake in Luanda’s multipurpose terminal under a 20-year concession and holds a 30% stake in the Dar es Salaam container terminal in Tanzania through a joint venture with Adani Ports and East Harbour Terminals. In August 2025, AD Ports also signed an agreement with Angola’s trade regulator, ARCCLA, to develop a digital Single Logistics Trade Window, alongside a six-million-dollar expansion of its local truck fleet under the Noatum Unicargas Logistics subsidiary. For 2026, the group has budgeted AED 2.45 billion (approximately 667 million dollars) in port infrastructure capital expenditure, according to its own investor presentations.
The investment logic extends well beyond the current security situation. Concessions running 20 to 30 years give Gulf operators direct control over terminal operations, replacing a model built on short-term agreements. Gulf states are no longer just acquiring stakes in African assets: they are assuming operational responsibility for the corridors that link African producers to global markets.
The Efficiency Gap African Ports Must Now Close
The scale of Gulf investment is not matched by uniform port performance across the continent. Wait times for vessels to offload cargo at Dar es Salaam can stretch to five days, compared to 1.25 days at Kenya’s Port of Mombasa, according to Trade Finance Global. That differential matters to shippers calculating total logistics costs and limits how much traffic a port can retain once the Red Sea becomes viable again.
Sameer Bhatnagar, global head of ports at KPMG, outlined the risk in ACCA’s AB Magazine in May 2026: “Without addressing these constraints, increased shipping volumes risk translating into congestion and higher logistics costs rather than economic benefit.” His list of urgent investment priorities included deep-water berths, port rail corridors, and digital upgrades to reduce cargo dwell times.
Ebrima Sawaneh, group COO and CFO at Arise Ports and Logistics, which manages concessions across West Africa, gave a candid sector-wide assessment: “A few African ports are clearly world class or close to it, but many others are still constrained.” If efficiency gaps persist, the traffic diverted from the Red Sea becomes a temporary windfall rather than a platform for lasting competitiveness.
The potential upside of closing those gaps is substantial. Trade Finance Global estimated that efficiency improvements across African port infrastructure could yield up to 5.3 billion dollars in total logistics-chain savings.
Infrastructure Arriving Before the Institutions
The corridors, terminals, and digital customs systems now under construction will be operational long after current Red Sea security dynamics have resolved. The Jebel Ali-Berbera route, the Ndayane deep-sea terminal, the Banana port in the DRC, and the Angola digital trade window are commitments locked in by operators working on generational time horizons.
For African coastal states and their regional bodies, the pressing question is whether institutional frameworks can be upgraded to match the capital now arriving. Customs harmonization between neighboring port states, accelerated port authority reform, and investment in port-adjacent rail infrastructure would all help domestic economies capture more of the value moving through their waters. The private capital is in place. The governance architecture to make full use of it is still being assembled, and the window to do so is not indefinite.

articles.title: DP World CEO urges India to rethink port concession model to attract long-term investment - India Shipping News
articles.summary: DP World CEO urges India to rethink port concession model to attract long-term investment  India Shipping News
articles.full_text:
DUBAI: DP World Group CEO Yuvraj Narayan has called for a fundamental rethink of India’s port development model, arguing that traditional time-bound concessions discourage long-term investment and that joint ventures between governments and private operators could deliver more sustained infrastructure development.
“A 30-year concession means what? Just look at the life cycle,” Narayan said, contending that it can take years to build a port and stabilise operations, leaving operators with a relatively short period of high utilisation in which to recover their investments and modernise facilities.
“Why not JVs? Become a landlord. You have an operator, you agree on KPIs. It’s forever, till I break your trust. What’s the problem?” he said.
Under the model he advocates, the government would retain ownership of the underlying port infrastructure while partnering with private operators through longer-term joint ventures, with performance measured against agreed targets.
Narayan argued that such arrangements could encourage operators to invest in capacity upgrades and technology without the uncertainty of repeated tenders and contract renewals.
His comments come as DP World seeks to expand its presence in India, where it has pledged an additional $5 billion in investment to strengthen its ports, rail and logistics network. The company has already invested about $3 billion in the country over three decades.
DP World’s Indian operations span five container terminals with a combined annual capacity of 6 million TEUs, warehousing, freight forwarding, container freight stations, free trade warehousing zones and inland rail terminals.
The company is also expanding its integrated logistics network, including through the second phase of Nhava Sheva Business Park in Maharashtra, backed by an investment of about ₹500 crore, and is exploring further opportunities in port infrastructure, including Vadhavan.
The investments are aimed at improving connectivity between ports and inland markets, facilitating trade and strengthening India’s role in global supply chains.
Narayan said the company was prepared to invest a further $3 billion to $5 billion as opportunities emerged, but called for faster project execution and more predictable frameworks for private participation.
He criticised arrangements in which operators invest in infrastructure while facing revenue-sharing demands, tariff controls and the prospect of competing facilities being developed nearby.
“If you have your own stake, would you do that? You are destroying value immediately,” he said.
India also needed a clearer assessment of existing port capacity and utilisation before committing to further expansion, Narayan said, adding that DP World’s own ports were operating at full capacity, unlike parts of the wider Indian port industry.
He said India should focus on becoming a gateway for its own exports and imports rather than pursuing transshipment volumes as an end in themselves.
“India should only wish to be a gateway. To be a transshipment is a bad investment,” he said, arguing that the economic benefits of transshipment – the transfer of cargo between ships – largely accrue to shipping lines rather than flowing into the wider domestic economy.
A gateway strategy, by contrast, would connect Indian manufacturers and consumers to international markets while generating demand for inland transport, warehousing and other logistics services.
The distinction is significant as India invests in large port projects intended to accommodate bigger vessels and improve direct connectivity to global shipping routes.
The government approved the Vadhavan port project in Maharashtra in June 2024 at an estimated cost of ₹76,220 crore, with planned container-handling capacity of about 23.2 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs). The project is designed to strengthen India’s maritime capacity and reduce dependence on overseas transshipment hubs.
Narayan said DP World would pursue opportunities in India’s port sector, including Vadhavan, while expanding its rail and inland logistics network.
He estimated that the Vadhavan project could entail about $10 billion in investment over 10 to 15 years, depending on its development phases.
Narayan’s call for a more durable infrastructure model comes as disruptions in West Asia expose vulnerabilities of global supply chains and increase the cost of moving goods.
He pointed out that restrictions on access to DP World’s Jebel Ali port in Dubai had disrupted a key logistics hub linking Asia with the Middle East, Africa and Europe. The consequences extended well beyond the Gulf, affecting cargo flows and creating congestion across other parts of the company’s network.
The disruption has reinforced the need for alternative shipping routes, additional capacity and more resilient supply chains, Narayan said, but warned that such measures would be expensive and could take years to implement.
Businesses that once prioritised lean inventories and just-in-time delivery are increasingly being forced to maintain alternative suppliers and routes, raising working-capital requirements and operating costs.
“Who do you think pays for all this disruption? You – as a consumer,” he said.
Narayan highlighted that globalisation had generated substantial wealth but distributed its benefits unevenly, contributing to political tensions and a broader breakdown in the international order.
He said the world was moving towards a more fragmented trading system without a clear replacement for the structures that had underpinned decades of global commerce.
He nevertheless expressed optimism that a political settlement would eventually emerge, saying DP World was willing to contribute to rebuilding damaged infrastructure and supply chains but was not positioned to drive international diplomacy.
Narayan also backed efforts to rebuild India’s domestic shipbuilding capabilities, describing a degree of self-sufficiency in strategically important industries as necessary.
Tie ups DP World has signed a memorandum of understanding with Cochin Shipyard to help develop maritime capabilities in India, he said.
The company is not itself a shipbuilder, but has expertise in ship repair, dry docks and engineering, procurement and construction services that could support the development of a broader maritime ecosystem.
On competition from Indian conglomerates investing in ports and logistics, Narayan said DP World’s international network offered a different proposition from businesses focused primarily on the domestic market.
“What is my offering to a business in India? … I can sell their hair extensions in Nigeria,” he said, illustrating how the company’s global connectivity could help Indian producers reach overseas customers.
For Narayan, the opportunity in India extends beyond building ports. It lies in linking domestic producers to international markets through an integrated network of maritime, rail and logistics assets – and in creating an investment framework that encourages private operators to keep improving those assets over the long term.

Nigeria and the United Kingdom have reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral relations and translating existing agreements into concrete outcomes across key sectors.
The commitment was made during a meeting between the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Dunoma Umar Ahmed, and the Director-General, Diplomatic Network, Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), Ms. Christiana Scott, in Abuja.

Spokesperson of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Oluwafemi Adeniyi, said in a statement on Tuesday.
Both sides identified the Defence and Security Partnership and the Migration, Justice and Home Affairs Dialogue as key frameworks for improving coordination and monitoring progress on shared priorities.
Ahmed highlighted opportunities for expanded cooperation in solid minerals, agriculture, renewable energy, transport and industry, stressing the importance of local value addition, technology transfer, job creation and sustainable economic growth.
He also called for improved access to the UK market through the relaxation of restrictions affecting Nigerian products.
The Permanent Secretary outlined the four Ds of President Tinubu’s foreign policy priorities: Demography, Development, Diaspora and Democracy, emphasising the strategic role of Nigerians in the diaspora in promoting economic cooperation and strengthening people-to-people relations.
He reaffirmed Nigeria’s commitment to African-led solutions to regional challenges, strengthening the African Union and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), and implementing the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to accelerate continental economic integration.
Ahmed stressed the need for a structured follow-up mechanism with clear timelines, institutional responsibilities and measurable targets to ensure the effective implementation of bilateral agreements.
In her remarks, Scott acknowledged Nigeria’s economic reform efforts and expressed the UK’s interest in facilitating greater participation by British businesses in emerging investment opportunities in Nigeria.
She disclosed plans for business engagements in Lagos, including discussions on investment opportunities in the port sector.
The UK official also reiterated her country’s commitment to supporting regional security and stability, particularly through its Sahel strategy, which prioritises diplomatic engagement, humanitarian assistance and economic resilience.
Both sides underscored the importance of addressing the underlying socio-economic causes of insecurity alongside conventional security measures.
They also reaffirmed their commitment to combating terrorism, violent extremism and transnational security threats through enhanced intelligence-sharing, technological support and institutional capacity-building.
The meeting further provided an opportunity to exchange views on democratic governance, credible electoral processes and the growing challenges posed by misinformation and artificial intelligence-generated content.
Discussions also covered preparations for the forthcoming Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda, including dialogue on the historical legacy of the transatlantic slave trade.
Other areas of cooperation included food security, rail infrastructure, electrification, climate action, green finance and agricultural value chains.
Both countries agreed to sustain diplomatic engagement, strengthen institutional cooperation and pursue practical partnerships for their mutual benefit.

articles.title: Türkiye part of region with $872B infrastructure project pipeline: HSBC | Daily Sabah - Daily Sabah
articles.summary: Türkiye part of region with $872B infrastructure project pipeline: HSBC | Daily Sabah  Daily Sabah
articles.full_text:
Türkiye is part of a region that has an $872 billion pipeline of infrastructure projects, highlighting its investment potential and offering international and corporate investors greater exposure to the region ahead of 2030, according to a report from HSBC.
Investment in alternative logistics routes could mitigate the impact of the Iran war and make the Strait of Hormuz "redundant" in the next five years, HSBC Group CEO Georges Elhedery told an event in Dubai on Tuesday.
The report, published Monday and based on data from MEED, a Dubai-based construction industry market intelligence platform, covers the Middle East, North Africa and Türkiye (MENAT) region.
The $872 billion is part of a wider infrastructure pipeline worth $1.4 trillion.
The Iran war has shown how heavily the world relies on the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway at the mouth of the Persian Gulf between Iran and Oman. A fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade previously passed through it.
The conflict is pushing Gulf nations to channel resources into energy pipelines to ports, Elhedery said. He said this investment will help the region weather the fallout.
"Of course, we do wish and hope to see a resolution to the conflict," he said, but "Hormuz, probably in five years' time, may become redundant."
"We do see this region being able to recover and then continue growing," he said. "It will mean a lot of investment."
A recent HSBC survey of over 1,600 business leaders and around 820 global institutional investors, meanwhile, found that they still considered the Gulf an attractive investment hub.
However, after growth of 3.3% in 2025, the World Bank last week forecast a deep economic contraction of 1.3% in the Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan region this year due to the war. That should be followed by a strong but uneven rebound in 2027.
HSBC's report doesn't say which Turkish projects are included in the $872 billion or how much of it is in Türkiye.
The country's place in the grouping reflects its role as a route between the Gulf and Europe.
The most direct example is the Development Road, a planned corridor linking the Persian Gulf to Europe through Iraq and Türkiye. It complements the Middle Corridor, the route across Central Asia and the Caucasus.
Cargo leaving Iraq's Faw Port, on the Gulf coast in Iraq's far south, would travel about 1,200 kilometers by rail to Ovaköy, a crossing on the Türkiye-Iraq border in southeastern Türkiye.
Turkish officials have linked that project to Hormuz and said that, had the Development Road been completed, the world's energy supply would have been far less affected.
Earlier this month, Türkiye opened the Çerkezköy-Kapıkule section, the longest part of the Halkalı-Kapıkule high-speed rail line, extending the network to the EU border.
The line is 229 kilometers long. It begins on Istanbul's western edge and ends at Türkiye's main rail and road border crossing with Bulgaria, at Kapıkule near the northwestern city of Edirne.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said the line is a key component of the 2,094-kilometer Turkish section of the Development Road.

articles.title: Zimbabwe’s Lithium Pivot: Promises and Pitfalls of Mining - The China-Global South Project
articles.summary: Zimbabwe’s Lithium Pivot: Promises and Pitfalls of Mining  The China-Global South Project
articles.full_text:
- Zimbabwe's lithium boom offers major value-capture potential but lacks coherent industrial policy and sufficient energy, water, and transport infrastructure.
- Communities endure pollution, displacement, and exclusion: limited skilled jobs, poor consultation, and weak Environmental Management Agency monitoring.
- February 2026 ban targets local beneficiation but risks investor uncertainty; urgent need for coherent policy, stronger governance, and Mutapa Investment Fund infrastructure financing.
By Julie Radomski and Tsitsi Musasike
Lithium has emerged as an indispensable resource powering the energy transition, given its central role in electric vehicle batteries and battery energy storage systems. For Zimbabwe, endowed with Africa’s largest lithium reserves, this presents a historic opportunity. The country accounted for nearly 10% of global lithium production in 2025.
The Zimbabwean government’s February 2026 ban on all raw mineral ore and lithium concentrate exports signals a more assertive push toward local beneficiation and local value capture. In principle, the measure strives to move Zimbabwe’s lithium sector beyond upstream extraction toward midstream processing and downstream industrial development. The policy also reshapes Zimbabwe’s engagement with foreign investors—particularly Chinese companies that currently dominate lithium mining operations and global refining capacity. Yet without a coherent national strategy or the infrastructure required to support refining and manufacturing, the ban may complicate investor engagement without guaranteeing greater domestic value addition.
In a new journal article on leveraging mineral extraction for Zimbabwe’s socio-economic development, translating its geological advantage into broad-based, sustainable development is an urgent governance challenge.
The Promise of a Lithium Boom
Mining has long been central to Zimbabwe’s economy, accounting for 14 percent of GDP, 75 percent of export earnings and 20 percent of government revenues in 2024, according to the World Bank Group. Lithium alone contributed $209 million to mining exports in 2023, with production increasing from just over 20,000 metric tons in 2020 to more than 826,000 metric tons in 2023. The government’s ambitious Vision 2030 relies in part on the mining sector as a pillar of growth to propel Zimbabwe into becoming an upper-middle income country.
This dramatic growth has attracted substantial foreign investment since 2021, particularly from China. Chinese companies are responsible for approximately 60 percent of the world’s lithium refining capacity and 70 percent of lithium-ion battery production. To sustain these industries, China imports much of the lithium it extracts from Australia, Chile, Argentina, and increasingly, Zimbabwe. Across all currently operating lithium mines in Zimbabwe, there is significant Chinese involvement in all six. Chinese private companies have invested over one billion dollars in acquiring and developing lithium projects in Zimbabwe since 2021. Several of these companies have also invested in processing plants to produce lithium sulphate in Zimbabwe, including Huayou Cobalt at the Arcadia mine, Yahua Group at Kamativi and Sinomine at Bikita.
Figure 1: Map of Lithium Mining Sites in Zimbabwe
Despite the boom in investment in the lithium sector, Zimbabwe lacks a standalone mining policy or transition mineral strategy to guide the sector’s growth, manage environmental and social risks, and map a course towards midstream, downstream, or sidestream development. Instead, Zimbabwe’s mining sector remains governed by the 1961 Mines and Minerals Act, a colonial-era legislation ill-suited to modern extractive governance. Although a revised Mines and Minerals Bill was gazetted in 2025, it has yet to be enacted and, moreover, is not crafted in line with a robust strategic policy framework.
The African Union’s Africa Mining Vision (AMV) outlines four interconnected streams in mineral development: upstream (extraction), midstream (processing and refining), downstream (manufacturing) and sidestream (infrastructure, skills and technology development). Currently, Zimbabwe remains overwhelmingly focused on upstream activities, with limited movement toward capturing value at subsequent stages.
The government’s 2022 ban on raw lithium exports and reported ban on lithium concentrate exports beginning in 2027 intended to promote local beneficiation, but in practice, loopholes have allowed raw ore to continue flowing abroad. The government subsequently announced the February 2026 immediate ban on export of all raw minerals and lithium concentrates after investigations revealed stockpiles of mineral ores at the Port of Beira in Mozambique.
The sudden announcement of the lithium concentrate export ban underscores the fragmented nature of mineral governance in Zimbabwe: ambitious policy signals are not yet matched by an integrated strategy for industrial development, infrastructure expansion or regulatory enforcement.
Instead, recent investment in the lithium sector has catalyzed production, but also raised environmental and social concerns. The report uses a mixed-method investigation—combining surveys of 230 respondents across all six mining sites with key stakeholder interviews—which paints a troubling picture of the lithium sector’s impact on development in practice.
Communities at the Frontline
While residents in the communities surrounding lithium mining sites acknowledge some employment and other economic opportunities, when asked about socio-economic development in their areas, 40 percent rated it as “poor,” 50 percent as “fair” and a mere 19 out of 230 respondents across all sites rated it positively (Figure 2). Employment opportunities for locals are concentrated in low-skilled and unskilled roles, with white-collar and technical opportunities remaining limited.
Figure 2: Responses on Whether the Area is Moving Forward in Terms of Socioeconomic Development
Further, survey results reveal profound dissatisfaction regarding local engagement. An overwhelming 94 percent of respondents reported feeling their input and feedback was not valued by mining companies, also identifying a lack of meaningful consultation or even communication on the part of these mines. This is a serious concern for communities across all mining sites, regardless of the ownership structure or nationality of the companies involved (see Figure 3).
Figure 3: Responses on Whether Community Input is Valued
Government officials and company representatives emphasize that Environmental and Social Impact Assessments are mandatory and are overseen by the Environmental Management Agency. However, civil society and survey data attest that implementation and ongoing monitoring is lacking. Air pollution (identified by 84% of respondents) and noise pollution (72%) top the list of environmental concerns, according to the results shown in Figure 4. In areas like Sandawana and Kamativi, land use change and appropriation emerged as significant issues (42% overall), with communities also reporting inadequate compensation and consultation during displacement or resettlement processes.
Figure 4: Environmental Concerns Regarding the Mining Sites
engagement with communities located near extraction sites is critical to ensure that local populations can access opportunities beyond low-skilled mining jobs as the sector evolves.
Infrastructure Bottlenecks
Infrastructure presents another critical challenge for both local communities and the mining industry. Companies are not legally obligated to provide public infrastructure, yet lithium mining’s expansion is itself contributing to straining Zimbabwe’s already fragile infrastructure. Roads serving the mining sites and surrounding areas, originally built for passenger traffic, are deteriorating under the weight of trucks transporting heavy ore. The research team documented a bus stuck on damaged road and excessive dust pollution on gravel routes to and/or near mines as shown in Figure 5. The country’s rail network is now largely defunct, forcing this unsustainable reliance on road transport.
Figure 5: Bus stuck on the road near Sandawana Mine
Beyond transport, energy and water infrastructure face similar pressures. While some companies have invested in last-mile transmission lines and substations (Bikita, Arcadia) or even coal-fired power plants (Sabi Star), these investments remain fragmented and primarily serve individual mining operations. If Zimbabwe intends to process lithium domestically, the mining policy raises urgent questions about whether the country’s infrastructure—particularly electricity, water and transport systems—can support energy-intensive refining operations.
The report calls for an integrated infrastructure development strategy, arguing that the Mutapa Investment Fund (MIF)—Zimbabwe’s sovereign wealth fund—could play a catalytic role as a co-financier in public-private partnerships (PPPs) for infrastructure. Established in 2015 and restructured in 2023, the MIF receives at least 25 percent of mining royalties and dividends from state-owned enterprises. By leveraging resource revenues and mining companies’ offtake guarantees, MIF could support rail rehabilitation, renewable energy and water management systems that benefit both industry and communities.
To achieve this, transparency, strong governance and political will are critical. Lessons from Norway’s sovereign wealth fund and emerging African examples like Ethiopia’s Industrial Holdings fund suggest that clear fiscal rules and independent oversight are essential for credibility and effectiveness.
Building an Inclusive Lithium Economy

articles.title: Canada commits $181m to Saint John port and rail upgrades - Splash247
articles.summary: Canada commits $181m to Saint John port and rail upgrades  Splash247
articles.full_text:
Canada has committed up to C$254m ($181m) in federal funding to expand cargo-handling capacity and improve rail connections at Port Saint John in New Brunswick.
The investment is intended to support the port’s expansion towards annual container-handling capacity of between 850,000 and 1m teu.
The programme includes dredging and marine infrastructure upgrades designed to accommodate larger vessels and increase the number of suitable high-water tidal windows for fully laden, deeper-draught ships by at least 30%.
Port warehouses will be expanded and upgraded, while a new container examination facility will be established for the Canada Border Services Agency.
Rail improvements include upgrading 103 km of the New Brunswick Southern Railway with continuously welded track, increasing mainline speeds to 64 km/h and improving connections between the port and North America’s Class I railway network.
The project will also stabilise the shoreline at the Bayshore Rail Terminal, protecting the port’s only rail access, and reconstruct the Simms Corner junction to separate road and rail traffic.
The funding is being provided through Canada’s Trade Diversification Corridors Fund.
The project involves the federal and New Brunswick governments, Port Saint John and New Brunswick Southern Railway.
